This paper investigates the connection between the algebraic characterization of functions and the computational characterization of typed lambda calculi. We demonstrate that a specific term rewriting system, derived from the simply typed lambda calculus and capable of computing all regular functions, corresponds to a monad on the category of sets and functions. Furthermore, we extend this correspondence to other term rewriting systems that can compute broader classes of functions beyond regularity. Finally, we introduce a new term rewriting system that computes all weakly holomorphic functions. As an application, we propose a new abstract machine designed to execute all regular functions. This machine, which is a superclass of the finite state transducer, is defined as a quadruple consisting of a set of states, a set of data, a transition function, and a data function. We provide a categorical characterization for these machines and establish an isomorphism between regular functions and this class of machines. Additionally, we characterize the data-free machines within this framework. The paper concludes with a discussion of the differences between stateful and stateless abstract machines.

Keywords: abstract computation, algebraic characterization, computational characterization, lambda calculus, higher order functions, finite state transducers, weakly holomorphic functions, abstract machines.

This brief note aims to demonstrate that the discrepancy between Itô and Stratonovich integrals, when applied to processes defined by conditional measure flows with functional integrands, corresponds precisely to the discrepancy between the measures on the space of conditional measure flows generated by these two integration methods. This correspondence holds for a specific class of functions defined on the space of conditional measure flows, a class that encompasses all functions of finite energy. The result is particularly significant for analyzing the renormalization of conditional measure flows. Furthermore, we derive the renormalization constant associated with the discrepancy between Itô and Stratonovich integrals for a particular functional of conditional measure flows, a specific instance of which is the time integral of the covariance of the flow. This specific case represents the discrepancy between the Itô and Stratonovich interpretations of the stochastic heat equation. We also examine the case of white noise and provide an alternative derivation of the renormalization constant for the discrepancy between the Itô and Stratonovich interpretations of the stochastic heat equation. Additionally, we address the renormalization of the time integral of the covariance of the conditional measure flow for the stochastic heat equation, a topic previously explored by the first author in [10]. Finally, we present an example of a function of a conditional measure flow that possesses infinite energy. In this scenario, the discrepancy between the Itô and Stratonovich integrals is identified as the covariance of the flow evaluated at zero, which diverges to infinity. Consequently, the renormalization constant for this discrepancy is also infinite. This example illustrates that the conditional measure flow of the stochastic heat equation exhibits anomalous behavior. We also provide an example of a function with finite energy whose discrepancy between the Itô and Stratonovich integrals is proportional to the covariance of the conditional measure flow of the stochastic heat equation at zero. This implies that the renormalization constant for this discrepancy is also infinite. We further demonstrate that the discrepancy between the Itô and Stratonovich integrals for a specific function of a conditional measure flow, which has finite energy, is zero. This finding suggests that the conditional measure flow of the stochastic heat equation does not display anomalous behavior. This paper introduces the concepts of finite, compact, and discrete normal spaces (referred to as finiteness, compactness, and discreteness) within the normal structure spaces of groups. The study examines these properties across various group categories, including finite, compact matrix, amenable, locally compact, profinite, and discrete topological groups. Additionally, the notions of final and initial normal structure spaces are defined and developed for groups. The work concludes by presenting several open problems in this emerging area. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that the normal structure spaces of the free group $F_2$, the group of all permutations of a set with three elements ($S_3$), and the group of all permutations of a set with two elements ($S_2$) are neither finite nor compact. Finally, the finite, compact, and discrete nature of normal structure spaces for the free group $F_2$ and the group $S_3$ are investigated. The paper also establishes that the normal structure spaces of the free group $F_2$, the group $S_3$, and the group $S_2$ are not homeomorphic to one another. Additionally, it is shown that the normal structure spaces of the free group $F_2$, the group $S_3$, and the group $S_2$ are not homeomorphic to any finite set. Finally, the study addresses the question of whether the normal structure spaces of the free group $F_2$, the group $S_3$, and the group $S_2$ are metrizable. The paper further develops the concepts of the normal structure space of a topological group and the normal structure functor, which maps topological groups to $T_1$-topological spaces. It is demonstrated that the normal structure functor is continuous. The continuity of this functor is utilized to characterize the normal structure spaces of finite groups, compact groups, discrete topological groups, and locally compact groups. Additionally, the continuity of the normal structure functor is employed to characterize the normal structure spaces of Hausdorff groups, Hausdorff abelian groups, and locally compact abelian groups. The paper also investigates the normal structure spaces of Hausdorff groups and Hausdorff abelian groups that possess the countable chain condition. Furthermore, the continuity of the normal structure functor is used to characterize the normal structure spaces of Tychonoff groups, Tychonoff abelian groups, and locally compact abelian groups. This study addresses the challenge of mapping natural language to SQL queries within a cross-domain context. While previous research has primarily focused on enhancing generalization capabilities, this work shifts its emphasis to improving precision. To achieve this, we introduce a novel cross-domain semantic parsing framework that integrates a domain-specific pre-training module with a multi-task learning approach. Additionally, we propose a new auxiliary task designed to boost the model's ability to capture domain-specific features. Extensive experiments conducted on the Spider benchmark demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/End-to-End-Cross-Domain-SQL-Parsing. Furthermore, the pre-trained model can be downloaded from https://drive.google.

This study introduces a data-driven, risk-sensitive approach to Model Predictive Control (MPC) designed for safe navigation within multi-robot systems. The proposed method utilizes a finite set of observed state and control trajectories to construct a data-driven probability distribution, which is subsequently integrated into the MPC cost function. This integration enables the robot to navigate safely among its peers by balancing operational performance with a tunable risk sensitivity parameter. Simulation results demonstrate that the method effectively prevents collisions and successfully guides robots toward their targets. Furthermore, the approach exhibits robustness against model uncertainties and ensures safe navigation even when initial conditions deviate from the training data distribution. The method's applicability to multi-robot systems is validated through simulations of a multi-floor office environment featuring multiple elevators. Additionally, the method is tested on a mobile robot navigating a real-world indoor setting. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/leeyongjun12345/DRSMPC. We report the discovery of a new ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, designated Andromeda XXV (And XXV), orbiting the Andromeda galaxy (M31). This system was identified through a deep, wide-field survey of the M31 halo utilizing the Pan-STARRS1 3.5-gigapixel digital survey camera. The galaxy exhibits a projected distance of 11.5 kpc from M31's center, a physical half-light radius of 12.4 parsecs, and a total luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^3 L_{\odot}$. Its stellar population is estimated to be approximately 10 Gyr old, with a metallicity of $[Fe/H] \sim -1.5$. We estimate the galaxy's dynamical mass within its half-light radius to be $M_{1/2} \sim 1.1 \times 10^7 M_{\odot}$, yielding a mass-to-light ratio of $\sim 10^4$. The derived mass profile indicates a low central dark matter density of $\rho_{DM} \sim 10^{-3} M_{\odot} \text{pc}^{-3}$, which is significantly lower than those found in other dwarf galaxies. This low density suggests that And XXV may have experienced a recent interaction with M31, such as a tidal encounter or a close flyby. Additionally, we estimate the galaxy's mass ratio to be $\sim 10^{-4}$, positioning it as the most massive ultra-faint dwarf galaxy known. Finally, we calculate the galaxy's orbital parameters, finding an orbital eccentricity of $\sim 0.5$ and a pericentric distance of $\sim 1.5$ kpc. These results imply that And XXV is on a highly eccentric orbit and has passed through the M31 tidal radius at least once. These findings support the hypothesis that And XXV is a recently accreted satellite of M31. Furthermore, the low central dark matter density observed in And XXV may be a common characteristic among galaxies recently accreted by the Milky Way and M31. This study underscores the value of deep, wide-field surveys for detecting and studying ultra-faint dwarf galaxies. Grant-free access is a promising technique for enabling massive connectivity in Internet of Things (IoT) networks, where devices transmit data without first requesting permission from the base station. This approach relies on designing sequences that are sufficiently distinct to allow the base station to reliably identify and separate them. This paper introduces a design method utilizing a two-stage genetic algorithm. In the first stage, sequences are generated by optimizing Hamming distance, while the second stage focuses on minimizing the normalized Hamming correlation matrix. The proposed method was benchmarked against existing techniques, including Golay complementary pairs, binary Golay sequences, and binary Kasami sequences. Simulation results demonstrate that the method outperforms these alternatives, achieving a 10 dB gain in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for a bit error rate (BER) of $10^{-3}$ and a 20 dB gain for a BER of $10^{-4}$. Furthermore, the method exhibits superior performance in low SNR environments and maintains robustness against variations in the number of devices and sequence length. Additionally, the method is applicable to both real-valued and complex-valued sequences. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/Two-Stage-Genetic-Algorithm}. Finally, the method is extensible to other sequence designs by incorporating other metrics into the fitness function. This design is particularly well-suited for IoT applications requiring massive connectivity. The paper is structured as follows: Section II outlines the system model; Section III details the proposed sequence design method; Section IV presents simulation results; and Section V offers concluding remarks. This study examines the thermodynamic modeling of moist air, focusing on two approximate frameworks: the saturation approximation and the mixing approximation. We demonstrate that both can be formulated as exact thermodynamic models for moist air, with each derived from a specific equation of state. Furthermore, we introduce the thermally consistent saturation approximation, which is shown to be equivalent to the widely utilized isentropic saturation approximation. Finally, we provide an exact representation of the saturation surface within these various models. The analysis relies exclusively on fundamental thermodynamic principles, avoiding any additional physical assumptions. Consequently, the findings are applicable to any moist air model, including those incorporating phase changes among multiple phases and water constituents. All derivations are implemented in the Python package `thermo`, which is accessible via PyPI. The package also provides an interface to the saturation surface for moist air. Additionally, we outline an approach for constructing approximate models for moist air in planetary atmospheres. This approach involves selecting an appropriate equation of state and subsequently deriving the corresponding approximate model for moist air. We illustrate this methodology using equations of state for dry air relevant to planetary atmospheres. The Python package `thermo` includes implementations of these specific models. Finally, we demonstrate how to utilize `thermo` to calculate the saturation surface for moist air. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the thermodynamic modeling of moist air; Section 3 presents the thermodynamic derivation of the thermally consistent saturation approximation; Section 4 details the thermodynamic derivation of the saturation surface for approximate models; Section 5 describes the equation of state for dry air utilized in the `thermo` package; Section 6 outlines the approach for constructing approximate models for moist air using the `thermo` package; and Section 7 concludes the paper. The `thermo` package is available on PyPI. The authors acknowledge the valuable discussions with members of the Planetary Atmospheres group at the University of Oxford. This paper extends the concepts of vector spaces and exterior powers to matroids. We demonstrate that our construction retains key properties of exterior powers on vector spaces, including canonical decompositions, Poincaré duality, and the relationship with the determinant of a matrix. Additionally, we explore applications within hyperplane arrangements and establish a combinatorial interpretation for Schur functions. A significant finding is that the collection of all Schur functions forms a polynomial basis for our exterior algebra. Furthermore, we introduce a combinatorial definition of exterior powers for matroids that aligns with the algebraic approach when applied to matroid representations over commutative rings. Finally, we outline an avenue for future research concerning the connection between our exterior power construction and combinatorial Hopf algebras. This research investigates the integration of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) outputs within dialogue state tracking. We introduce a novel method that models ASR ambiguity using confusion networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating this confusion network representation enhances dialogue state tracking performance. Our findings indicate that the confusion network layer effectively captures ASR ambiguity, thereby boosting the accuracy of subsequent layers in the end-to-end pipeline. Additionally, we show that the proposed confusion network layer can be seamlessly integrated into existing systems without necessitating retraining of other components. Experimental results confirm that our approach yields significant performance gains, achieving a 2.5% increase in exact match scores. The computed values align with the Donaldson-Verlinde formula and the Euler characteristics of moduli spaces for rank-2 stable sheaves with a fixed determinant. A access structure is defined as a collection of subsets of a universal set that includes the universal set itself and remains closed under set intersection. In cooperative game theory, this concept corresponds to an intersection-closed family of coalitions. This paper examines the computational complexity of determining whether a specific access structure possesses certain properties. We establish that for any access structure $\mathcal{F}$, checking if there exists a subset $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ such that the Shapley value of $\mathcal{G}$ is contained within the Shapley value of $\mathcal{F}$ is an NP-complete problem. Additionally, we demonstrate that deciding whether a given access structure $\mathcal{F}$ can be expressed as the union of two access structures $\mathcal{G}_1$ and $\mathcal{G}_2$, where both $\mathcal{G}_1$ and $\mathcal{G}_2$ are subsets of $\mathcal{F}$, is also NP-complete. Finally, we prove that verifying if a given access structure $\mathcal{F}$ possesses the property of submodularity is NP-complete. In each instance, the access structures are represented as oracles. Furthermore, we explore the complexity of these problems when access structures are represented explicitly. We also investigate the complexity of identifying access structures with specific properties when they are represented implicitly through a given collection of sets. Finally, we outline the complexity of finding access structures with particular properties when they are represented explicitly. Throughout this work, we analyze the complexity of verifying properties for access structures defined as intersection-closed families of coalitions. We also consider the complexity of finding access structures with specific characteristics when they are defined as union-closed families of coalitions. In all cases, we examine the complexity of these problems under both explicit and implicit representations of the access structures. The paper concludes with an overview of the relationships between the various problems discussed.

Optimal measurement techniques are essential for characterizing quantum systems, yet achieving these measurements remains difficult due to the need for precise control and the development of sophisticated hardware. This study examines the estimation of entanglement within an optical two-qubit system. We demonstrate that the entanglement fidelity can be determined with optimal precision using a straightforward hardware configuration. This approach requires only a single interferometer setup, eliminating the need for repeated measurements across various configurations. We validate the method's effectiveness through experimental results. Furthermore, we explore strategies to enhance precision by leveraging prior knowledge of the target state. These findings offer a practical framework for optimal state estimation in photonic quantum systems. Additionally, the proposed scheme is applicable to other entangled states, such as Bell diagonal states, which are vital for quantum communication protocols. Our results pave the way for more efficient and precise state estimation in photonic quantum technologies. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this work to other platforms, including trapped ions and superconducting qubits. Overall, this research provides a valuable resource for advancing state estimation techniques in quantum technology. By enabling more accurate and efficient measurements, our findings can contribute to the development of practical quantum applications. This study examines the genesis and characteristics of Palm Tree Modes (PTMs) observed in JET discharges utilizing DIII-D hybrid scenarios. PTMs are identified as a specific class of Neoclassical Tearing Modes (NTMs) that develop under conditions of high toroidal magnetic field ($B_t$) and low plasma current ($I_p$). The analysis employs a linear NTM model incorporating neoclassical effects, which predicts PTMs as a distinct solution arising from the interaction between neoclassical resonance and the $q=2$ rational surface. This mechanism is validated through numerical simulations of JET discharges, which demonstrate the formation of PTMs and reveal their unique properties. Specifically, PTMs exhibit a $q=2$ magnetic island with a broad radial profile and a prominent peak at the edge. Furthermore, the study explores the stability of PTMs by analyzing the impact of neoclassical effects on their growth rates. Finally, the paper outlines the conditions under which PTMs are expected to appear in tokamaks with DIII-D-like configurations. These findings offer valuable insights into the formation of PTMs and suggest that they may be prevalent in tokamaks operating with high $B_t$ and low $I_p$. This could facilitate the development of more accurate models for PTM growth and provide a basis for predicting their onset in future tokamak discharges. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of NTMs and their influence on tokamak plasma performance. This understanding is crucial for the optimization of plasma scenarios in current and future tokamaks, including those equipped with advanced control systems. By elucidating the origins and characteristics of PTMs, this work paves the way for more effective control strategies, thereby enhancing the overall performance of tokamak plasmas. Additionally, the insights gained from this study may inform the design and operation of next-generation tokamaks, such as ITER and future fusion reactors. Understanding the role of PTMs in these advanced systems could lead to the development of new control techniques and the optimization of plasma scenarios for improved performance and stability. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader goal of achieving sustained fusion energy production through the advancement of tokamak technology. By elucidating the mechanisms behind PTMs, this work supports the ongoing efforts to harness the full potential of nuclear fusion as a viable and sustainable energy source for the future. Addressing the challenges of catastrophic forgetting and rehearsal in continual learning, we introduce a straightforward baseline that leverages the incremental nature of tasks to mitigate forgetting. Our approach utilizes a rehearsal buffer to store samples from previous tasks and employs a rehearsal strategy that refreshes this buffer with new data at the start of each subsequent task. We evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that it surpasses state-of-the-art techniques that depend on pretrained models. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/Simple-Baseline. The paper can be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01109. Our findings indicate that the incremental learning paradigm is inherently capable of addressing catastrophic forgetting, thereby questioning the necessity of incorporating pretrained models in continual learning scenarios. We hope this perspective inspires further research into the fundamental principles of continual learning. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We demonstrate that incremental learning can effectively tackle catastrophic forgetting, challenging the conventional reliance on pretrained models; (2) We offer a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between rehearsal size and performance; (3) We provide a detailed examination of the impact of rehearsal strategies on continual learning outcomes. This study addresses the challenge of detecting hate speech across various social media platforms by leveraging multi-modal data, specifically textual content and user avatars. We introduce a deep learning framework that integrates Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for avatar analysis with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for text processing. To ensure model transparency, we apply SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) to identify the most significant features within each modality. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework surpasses existing single-modal baselines in both performance and interpretability. Furthermore, we find that while textual features are more critical for identifying hate directed at women, visual features are more pivotal when the target is the LGBTQ community. This study examines how heterogeneity in neuronal degree distributions influences the synchronization of type-I neurons connected via random links. We begin by deriving the mean-field equations governing the evolution of the order parameter, which characterizes synchronization, for both homogeneous and heterogeneous networks. Subsequently, we analyze how these varying degree distributions impact the system's dynamical behavior. Our results indicate that while synchronization transitions are sharper in heterogeneous networks compared to homogeneous ones, the latter exhibit a broader range of parameter values conducive to synchronization. Furthermore, we observe that the steady-state values of the order parameter are generally higher in heterogeneous networks than in their homogeneous counterparts. Finally, we demonstrate that the steady-state solutions of the order parameter in heterogeneous networks can display complex patterns, including period-doubling bifurcations and chaotic dynamics. These findings underscore the critical role of network heterogeneity in shaping the dynamical properties of neuronal networks. Additionally, we show that the complex dynamics observed in this model can be replicated in a biological system composed of biological neurons. These outcomes highlight the significance of network heterogeneity in the context of biological neuronal networks. We construct an adversarial training environment where a generator creates adversarial patches to challenge a solver. This paper establishes the capacity region for a two-user Gaussian interference channel with decode-and-forward (GIFC-D-F) using an achievable random scheme. Leveraging this result, we derive the capacity region for a two-user Gaussian interference channel with decode-and-forward (GIFC-D-F) under the condition that one user transmits via decode-and-forward while the other employs compress-and-forward. Additionally, we determine the capacity region for a two-user Gaussian interference channel with compress-and-forward (GIFC-C-F) by assuming that the achievable random scheme for GIFC-D-F remains achievable in the C-F scenario. Finally, we demonstrate that the capacity region for a two-user Gaussian interference channel with compress-and-forward (GIFC-C-F) is attainable through a time-sharing strategy. These findings are achieved by applying the information spectrum approach to interference channel capacity analysis. Furthermore, the proposed achievable random scheme for GIFC-D-F is designed to be robust against channel state information (CSI) uncertainty at the receivers, thereby enhancing its practical applicability. The paper concludes with a discussion on the implications of these results.

Keywords: Gaussian interference channel, decode-and-forward, compress-and-forward, information spectrum approach, CSI uncertainty.

We introduce a novel technique for analyzing 3-dimensional flow data, designed to probe the collision geometry and the equation of state (EOS). This approach relies on a new metric termed the "flow field," derived from the 3-dimensional flow vector field. By examining the spatial distribution of the flow field, we can identify the collision geometry and estimate the maximum pressure generated during the interaction. We apply this method to Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV, comparing results from ideal hydrodynamic simulations using two distinct EOS models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 3-dimensional flow field is sensitive to the initial spatial anisotropy of the collision. Finally, we discuss the potential of this framework for investigating the initial state of the collision. Our findings indicate that this method is a valuable addition to existing 3-dimensional flow analysis tools, offering a complementary perspective on the system's evolution. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a type of neural network designed to process graph-structured data, making them highly effective for various wireless communication tasks such as channel estimation, multi-user detection, and interference mitigation. However, the graph structures required by GNNs are often static and predefined, which limits their flexibility. To address this, we propose a novel framework for decentralized GNN inference within wireless communication systems. In this approach, a graph is represented as a set of communicating nodes, where each node performs local computations and exchanges information with its neighbors. Consequently, the system becomes fully decentralized, eliminating the need for a central server. We demonstrate the viability of this framework through channel estimation, where a set of transmitters sends signals to receivers in the presence of additive noise. Our results indicate that the performance of this decentralized framework is nearly identical to that of a centralized system. Furthermore, we show that this framework can be realized using a specific class of physical layer protocols known as Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA). Finally, we outline the framework's potential applications in wireless communication systems. To our knowledge, this is the first work to introduce such a framework for GNN inference. Accelerated Stochastic Gradient Descent (ASGD) is a widely used optimization method for large-scale machine learning, offering a superior convergence rate compared to standard Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). However, ASGD is sensitive to various data-induced noise types, such as those arising from mini-batch sampling, label noise, and feature noise. This paper introduces a novel, unified framework for developing ASGD variants that are adaptive to both environmental noise and specific problems. The proposed framework is general, capable of accommodating diverse noise models and problem characteristics. We demonstrate that this approach can address multiple noise types and problem-adaptive scenarios, including nonconvex optimization. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithm achieves the optimal convergence rate for strongly convex problems across all considered noise models. Extensive experiments on large-scale linear regression and matrix completion tasks confirm the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/NoiseAdaptiveASGD. Finally, we anticipate that this work will inspire further research into adaptive ASGD algorithms tailored for specific problems and noise conditions. In contrast, "problem-adaptive" refers to the ability to achieve the optimal convergence rate across a broad class of problems, while "noise-robust" indicates the capacity to attain the optimal rate under a single, fixed noise model. Our proposed method is both problem-adaptive and noise-adaptive. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method is also noise-robust, a property that has not been previously established for any ASGD variant. We introduce and examine a novel category of self-oscillating systems. Distinct from classical self-oscillators, where a potential well migrates within a fixed background, our oscillators feature a potential well that evolves dynamically in response to the oscillator's own position and velocity. The motion of this class exhibits rich behavior, including period doubling bifurcations and chaos, and can be understood through a Poincaré map defined on a time-varying manifold. Both analytical and numerical methods are employed to study this new oscillatory phenomenon. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain members of this class display self-oscillatory behavior, serving as a straightforward model for active matter. Active matter encompasses a broad spectrum of systems, ranging from biological entities like bacteria and cells to larger structures such as flocks of birds, schools of fish, and even crowds of people. These systems are characterized by a significant proportion of their constituents consuming energy to generate forces that drive the system away from thermodynamic equilibrium. Consequently, they can spontaneously form structures that would be impossible under thermodynamic equilibrium conditions. Our findings suggest that the self-oscillatory systems identified herein could serve as a fundamental building block for constructing more complex forms of active matter. Additionally, we have created a self-propelled particle model based on these self-oscillators and conducted numerical simulations to investigate the collective dynamics of groups of such particles. The results indicate that these particles can form various types of structures, including ordered and disordered ones, and that these formations can be analyzed using standard techniques from active matter research. This suggests that the self-oscillatory systems we have identified may play a crucial role in the formation of structures within active matter systems. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research, including the development of analytical methods to describe the collective behavior of these systems and the exploration of their potential applications in technology and engineering. For instance, the self-oscillatory systems we have identified could be utilized to create new types of sensors or actuators. By harnessing the ability of these systems to generate forces that drive them away from thermodynamic equilibrium, it may be possible to design devices that are more efficient and effective than those currently available. In conclusion, the self-oscillatory systems we have identified represent a new and exciting area of research with the potential to significantly advance our understanding of active matter and lead to the creation of innovative technological devices. As such, we believe that further investigation into these systems is warranted. This research has the potential to deepen our comprehension of active matter

Robot dexterous grasping is a critical dexterous manipulation task that demands a robot's hand to adapt to various object shapes, sizes, and orientations. While dexterous grasping has been extensively researched, the majority of existing studies rely on either simulated or real-world data, with limited overlap between the two. This paper introduces DexGraspNet, a new large-scale dexterous grasp dataset comprising 100,000 samples. We developed this dataset using a novel dexterous hand model, the SoftHand, which features a soft, finger-like structure capable of grasping objects of diverse shapes, sizes, and orientations. The dataset was generated through a novel approach combining a large collection of 3D objects with a new dexterous hand model. To facilitate the training of dexterous hand policies, we propose a new training method that leverages the inherent properties of the hand model. Our experiments demonstrate that policies trained on DexGraspNet achieve superior performance in both simulation and real-world environments compared to those trained on existing datasets. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-compensated 4D (3D spatial dimensions plus respiration phase) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TSE) sequence designed for body imaging. The approach integrates a variable flip angle (VFA) scheme with a respiration-triggered acquisition method. To achieve robust motion compensation, a multi-shot readout strategy is employed, utilizing a self-navigated, data-driven approach that incorporates a novel, computationally efficient motion model. This model enables the reconstruction of motion-compensated 4D images with high temporal resolution, ranging from 1.5 to 3.0 seconds. The technique was evaluated using both in vitro phantoms and in vivo scans on a 3T clinical MRI system. Results demonstrated that the proposed method effectively corrects for both rigid and non-rigid motion artifacts in 4D images, yielding superior image quality compared to single-shot sequences. Furthermore, the method exhibits high robustness against motion, maintaining stable image quality even when the number of shots per readout is reduced. These findings suggest that this approach holds significant potential for enhancing the quality of 4D T2-weighted TSE imaging in clinical settings. We examine a dry-land vegetation model featuring grazing by an evolving population of functional responses that exhibit non-local dependence on plant biomass. This framework integrates both size-structured vegetation dynamics and grazing population dynamics. By applying bifurcation analysis, we identify several critical transitions, including saddle-node, Hopf, and grazing-induced bifurcations. Our findings indicate that an increase in grazing pressure can trigger a grazing-induced bifurcation, resulting in a sudden surge in the grazing population and a corresponding decline in plant biomass. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these grazing-induced bifurcations can be suppressed by enhancing the resilience of plant biomass. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for managing grazing systems. These conclusions are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the model equations and prove the global stability of the Hopf bifurcation. This work represents the first investigation into non-local grazing effects within a grazing model. The model's versatility allows it to address various grazing scenarios, such as those involving free-grazing animals, fixed stock levels, or human-controlled grazing. Our results underscore the necessity of accounting for non-local grazing effects when managing grazing systems. Furthermore, we show that the grazing population can undergo a grazing-induced bifurcation, leading to a sharp increase in animals and a consequent significant reduction in plant biomass. These insights are crucial for sustainable grazing management. Finally, we highlight the importance of considering plant biomass resilience in grazing systems and its role in preventing overgrazing. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of grazing effects, providing valuable insights for grazing management. Ultimately, our work demonstrates the efficacy of grazing management in maintaining ecological balance and the long-term sustainability of grazing systems. These findings are essential for achieving ecological stability and supporting the livelihoods of millions of people worldwide. Our research underscores the significance of grazing management in fostering a healthy ecosystem and a sustainable future. By implementing appropriate grazing strategies, we can ensure the continued existence of both plant and animal populations. This study provides a solid foundation for future research into grazing management and its impact on ecosystems. Ultimately, our work offers a valuable contribution to the field of grazing management, with the potential to shape policy decisions and guide practical applications. CountSketch is a widely used streaming algorithm designed to estimate the number of distinct elements in a stream. This algorithm is particularly valuable for large-scale data processing because it offers superior space efficiency compared to other streaming techniques. However, its theoretical guarantees rely on the assumption that input data is non-adaptive, meaning the distribution remains independent of the algorithm's internal randomness. This paper investigates the breakdown of CountSketch when faced with adaptive inputs. We demonstrate that for any fixed number of sketches $k$, an adaptive adversary can easily compromise the algorithm's accuracy. Furthermore, we establish that if the adversary is permitted to adaptively choose the number of sketches, the only method to ensure accurate estimates is to allocate an infinite number of sketches. Finally, we present a more nuanced analysis of the problem's complexity by examining the specific capabilities of the adversary. Our findings indicate that even a weak adversary can significantly degrade the performance of CountSketch. These results are derived through a combination of algorithmic constructions and advanced tools from probability theory and combinatorics. Additionally, we provide a practical evaluation of CountSketch under adaptive conditions, which aligns with our theoretical predictions. This section also explores the potential of various modifications to CountSketch for maintaining robustness against adaptive inputs. The code for our experiments is available at \url{https://github.com/robertkrawczyk/countsketch-adversarial}. The vendor can either enforce a uniform wholesale price for all intermediaries or implement a screening mechanism to assign prices selectively. Buyers are heterogeneous in their valuation, and the vendor's information regarding these valuations is limited; specifically, the vendor knows only the joint distribution of buyer types across different intermediaries. Buyers are partitioned into types based on their valuation levels and the specific intermediary they join. The vendor's objective is to maximize revenue by choosing between a wholesale pricing strategy or a screening approach. We analyze the optimal pricing structure for both scenarios and compare their resulting revenues. Our findings indicate that the vendor's information advantage is a critical determinant of the optimal strategy. When buyers associated with a specific intermediary are predominantly high-valuation types, that intermediary will likely undercut the wholesale price, causing the vendor to incur losses. Conversely, if the information advantage is significant, wholesale pricing becomes the superior strategy. Furthermore, we explore how the vendor can leverage this information edge to negotiate more favorable wholesale terms with intermediaries. We calculate exact expressions for the energies of two quasiparticles and two quasiholes, as well as the energy associated with a quasihole-electron pair. These precise analytical outcomes are achieved through the application of the Weyl algebra. Additionally, we provide an approximate analytical expression for the Jastrow factor concerning two quasiparticles. Finally, we compare these analytical results with exact numerical computations. Additionally, we offer an approximate analytical expression for the Jastrow factor regarding two quasiparticles in the Moore-Read state. Our findings have significant implications for quasiparticle-quasiparticle scattering and Coulomb blockade experiments. Stokes variational inequalities (SVIs) are frequently employed to model the motion of viscous fluids interacting with a rigid body. While recent research has established convergence results for mixed finite element approximations of SVIs under glaciological boundary conditions, these findings rely on the strong coercivity of the bilinear form associated with the Stokes equations. We identified a compact, bright continuum source at the galaxy's center, which we attribute to a central outflow. This outflow exhibits a flat spectral energy distribution (SED) across the 1.1–1.3 mm wavelength range, with a flux density of 1.0 ± 0.1 mJy at 1.2 mm. The emission is highly concentrated, with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 1.2 arcseconds (approximately 100 pc at the galaxy's distance). Furthermore, the outflow's momentum rate exceeds that of the galaxy's rotation, indicating that feedback processes are the primary driver of the galaxy's dynamics. The rapid expansion of connected and autonomous vehicles (CVs) has created a demand for intelligent, data-driven solutions to enhance road safety and traffic efficiency. However, the vast amounts of data generated by CVs introduce significant privacy and security risks. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a unified framework for privacy-preserving edge intelligence at the CV network level. This framework integrates three core technologies: federated learning (FL), differential privacy (DP), and secure aggregation (SA). FL enables the training of a global model using local data without requiring data sharing, while DP safeguards individual user privacy by managing the trade-off between privacy loss and model accuracy. SA further protects user data during the FL training process. The proposed framework is designed to be flexible, supporting various FL configurations, DP strategies, and aggregation methods. Additionally, we develop a specific implementation of this framework that incorporates a Byzantine-resilient FL algorithm, a heterogeneous CV network model, and a novel privacy-preserving data selection strategy. This strategy ensures that only data meeting specific privacy thresholds are selected for model training. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the framework and evaluate its performance through extensive simulations. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework can train a global model with high accuracy while maintaining robust privacy guarantees. Furthermore, our privacy-preserving data selection approach effectively mitigates privacy risks, achieving a balance between privacy protection and model accuracy. Finally, we show that the framework can successfully identify and isolate malicious CVs within the network. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to propose such a framework for privacy-preserving edge intelligence in vehicular networks. Extensive simulations confirm that the framework is highly effective in safeguarding CV privacy while delivering superior performance. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2000/PP-FL}. This paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews related work; Section III outlines the system model; Section IV details the proposed framework; Section V provides a theoretical analysis; Section VI presents simulation results; and Section VII concludes the paper. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We propose a novel privacy-preserving edge intelligence framework for CV networks that combines FL, DP, and SA; (2) We develop a specific implementation of this framework that addresses challenges related to data selection, heterogeneous network modeling, and malicious CV detection; (3) We provide a detailed theoretical analysis of the framework, including a new theoretical bound for the privacy leakage of the proposed data selection method. This finding extends the results established by Bak and van der Kallen. Additionally, we establish that $NK_1GQ(Gr(R))=0$ for any connected graded ring $Gr(R)$. Leveraging these findings, we derive a relative version of Bak's unitary determinant. Specifically, for a commutative ring $R$ with identity and a quadratic $Q$-filtration $\mathcal{F}$ on ${\rm Gr}_{\bullet}(R)$, we construct a determinant map:
$$\det_{UQ}: {\rm GSp}_{2n}({\rm Gr}_{\bullet}(R),\mathcal{F})\longrightarrow {\rm Wh}_{1}({\rm Gr}_{\bullet}(R),\mathcal{F}),$$
where ${\rm Wh}_{1}({\rm Gr}_{\bullet}(R),\mathcal{F})$ denotes the Whittaker group of ${\rm Gr}_{\bullet}(R)$ relative to $\mathcal{F}$. This map serves as the graded analogue to the determinant map defined by Bak. Finally, utilizing the determinant map, we prove that $NK_1GQ({\rm Gr}_{\bullet}(R),\mathcal{F})=0$. $$\det_{UQ}: {\rm GSp}_{2n}({\rm Gr}_{\bullet}(A),\mathcal{F})\longrightarrow {\rm Wh}_{1}({\rm Gr}_{\bullet}(A),\mathcal{F}).$$
This outcome extends the work of Bak and the second author. Finally, we provide an example demonstrating that the kernel of the determinant map is not necessarily trivial.

This work investigates how off-shell effects influence the extraction of the top quark mass from $t\bar{t}$+jet (ttj) events. We assess the significance of these effects by comparing two distinct methods for modeling them. Our findings indicate that incorporating off-shell contributions is essential for accurately simulating ttj data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the difference between these two approaches is substantial, suggesting that the standard procedure for including these effects may require reevaluation. Finally, we quantify the resulting uncertainty in the top quark mass determination. This uncertainty is significant and could potentially hinder the detection of new physics at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). Additionally, we observe that the uncertainty associated with the modeling of off-shell effects is not negligible compared to other systematic uncertainties, such as those arising from parton shower modeling. Consequently, we advocate for the development of new ttj analyses that employ more precise methods for modeling off-shell effects. Such advancements would enable a more robust determination of the top quark mass and facilitate a clearer search for new physics. To support this, we have released a public tool capable of accurately modeling off-shell effects in ttj events. This tool is available at \url{https://github.com/ulrikaschmitt/OffShellEffects}. It is built upon the \texttt{MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO} framework and utilizes the \texttt{MadLoop} plugin to calculate one-loop self-energy corrections for the top quark propagator. We demonstrate that this approach yields results consistent with those from the widely used \texttt{PropagatorVertex} method. Appendix \ref{app:loopcalc} provides technical details regarding the calculation of off-shell effects. Furthermore, the research investigates the impact of various parameter settings on the algorithm's effectiveness. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/APEA. The findings indicate that the proposed approach is highly effective and holds significant potential for application in other optimization contexts. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in learning from graph-structured data, their "black box" characteristics often hinder trust and usability. To address this, we introduce PGExplainer, a novel explainability framework designed to generate human-understandable explanations for GNN predictions. This method identifies a sparse subgraph and assigns node-level attention weights to highlight the specific features most critical to a given prediction. We formulate the problem as a parameterized combinatorial optimization task and develop a scalable, differentiable solver to simultaneously optimize the GNN and explainability objectives. Furthermore, we propose a new joint training strategy that leverages data augmentation to enhance both model performance and explanation quality. Extensive experiments across various graph classification benchmarks and real-world datasets confirm that PGExplainer effectively balances high accuracy with interpretability. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/dotmai/pgexplainer.

Substructure analysis of galaxy clusters is essential for understanding their formation and evolution. This study utilizes X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and optical data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey to investigate the substructure within the cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420. We applied the Caustic technique to determine the mass profile and identify substructures, while also employing the Caustic Gravitation Lensing method to estimate the mass of these features. Our findings reveal that the cluster's core is dominated by a central substructure, with a mass of $1.1 \times 10^{15} M_{\odot}$ and a redshift of $z=0.311$. Additionally, we identified four other substructures located at distances of 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, and 2.5 Mpc from the core, with masses ranging from $1.0 \times 10^{14} M_{\odot}$ to $2.0 \times 10^{14} M_{\odot}$ and redshifts between $z=0.29$ and $z=0.33$. The mass profile of RXCJ0232.2-4420 exhibits a steep decline at small radii, indicating a steep density profile, and a flattening at large radii, suggesting a transition to an isothermal density profile. Finally, we calculated the cluster's dynamical state using the Caustic Gravitation Lensing method, finding that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is in a relaxed state. These results suggest that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is a relaxed cluster that has recently undergone a merger. The findings from this study will be utilized in future research to further explore the cluster's dynamical state. The Chandra data utilized in this work were obtained from the Chandra Data Archive. The Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) is a recently introduced recurrent neural network module designed to enhance long-term memory capabilities. While the LMU achieves state-of-the-art results on various benchmarks, training its memory mechanisms remains computationally intensive. This paper introduces a parallelization strategy for training LMUs that leverages multi-core CPUs. Our approach demonstrates that training can be accelerated by a factor of 10 compared to a single-core CPU, and by a factor of 2.5 when using a CPU with four or more cores relative to a single-core CPU. Furthermore, we show that our method yields a 4.5-fold speedup compared to the current state-of-the-art parallelization technique on a CPU with four or more cores. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to the task of training an LMU-based language model. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/DeepMind/lmupar. We investigate the development of coherent communication within the naming game by incorporating the dynamics of social migration. Within this framework, agents interact to negotiate labels for new vocabulary through the naming game, while simultaneously migrating between two distinct communities. Our analysis demonstrates that this migration process significantly influences the system's evolution. Specifically, even when initial communities possess different pre-established vocabularies, the migration drives the formation of a shared, unified vocabulary across both groups. Furthermore, we show that the speed of this convergence is contingent upon the migration rate, which dictates the timescale required for the system to reach consensus. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Ultimately, our results indicate that social migration plays a crucial role in the emergence of a common language. Additionally, the proposed model offers a valuable framework for exploring the evolution of language and communication within social groups. Finally, we highlight the model's potential applications in various contexts, including the EU's efforts to foster a pan-European identity and the challenges of inter- and intra-organizational communication. These applications underscore the model's significance in advancing our understanding of language evolution and its impact on social dynamics. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a powerful method for addressing inverse problems in science and engineering. However, their practical application is often hindered by slow convergence and the inability to converge at all when dealing with problems characterized by strong spectral bias. This study investigates the impact of gradient descent momentum on PINNs convergence, revealing that momentum significantly mitigates spectral bias effects. We validate this finding through both numerical experiments and a theoretical analysis of the ReLU activation function under momentum conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating momentum into the Adam optimizer enhances its performance on inverse problems with spectral bias, achieving up to a 10x speedup compared to Adam without momentum. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Momentum-PINNs. This research underscores the critical role of momentum in accelerating PINNs convergence and offers a valuable tool for solving inverse problems involving spectral bias. Additionally, our findings provide a theoretical explanation for the superior performance of Adam with momentum in learning ReLU networks. We introduce a novel method for investigating spin-dependent dark matter interactions by utilizing the non-zero nuclear spin of individual $^6$Li atoms. This approach employs a $^6$LiF target within a direct dark matter detection experiment, leveraging the fact that each $^F$ nucleus possesses a non-zero nuclear spin. Blind image deblurring aims to recover a sharp image from a blurred input without prior knowledge of the blur parameters. This paper introduces a novel deblurring technique that leverages the relationship between images sharing similar content. The proposed method models the deblurring process as a kernel regression task, where a regression kernel is derived from a data-driven representation of image patches. To effectively capture the non-linear, low-rank structure inherent in these patches, we employ a kernel function based on the singular value thresholding operator. This approach yields a regression kernel that is both data-driven and non-linear, enabling the method to robustly reconstruct sharp images even when blur kernels are unknown. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the method exhibits strong generalization capabilities, successfully handling both single-image deblurring and deblurring in sequences. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/krdeblur. The source code will be integrated into the upcoming open-source deep learning toolkit, PyTorch. Additionally, the method is fully compatible with the widely used benchmark dataset, DAVIS. These contributions underscore the method's versatility and its potential for future advancements in the field. This paper introduces natural Hoare logic, a formal system designed for verifying programs based on specifications expressed in a natural language-like formalism. We demonstrate that the soundness and terminating completeness of the logic rely crucially on the presence of a focus mechanism within these specifications. Furthermore, we propose a proof system for a calculus incorporating focus and provide a type assignment system for the language alongside its logic. Finally, we illustrate the application of this proof system through examples derived from the formal specifications of the consensus algorithm within the Paxos framework. The paper concludes by outlining several avenues for future research.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model derived from the ADM Hamiltonian. The resulting quantum cosmological framework is formulated as a difference equation. We demonstrate that this equation admits a solution expressible as a power series in the variable $\beta$, where the series coefficients correspond to the coefficients of the $\beta$-expansion in the WKB approximation method. Furthermore, we establish that this $\beta$-expansion solution aligns with the solution previously obtained via the Holst Hamiltonian. Finally, we show that both solutions predict the same big-bang scenario. Additionally, we note that the solution derived from the ADM Hamiltonian yields a different expression for the quantum correction term compared to that from the Holst Hamiltonian. However, we argue that this discrepancy does not significantly impact the analysis of the quantum big-bang scenario. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision applications, yet their inability to quantify prediction uncertainty hinders their deployment in safety-critical environments. To address this, we introduce BayesOD, a Bayesian framework designed to estimate uncertainty in object detection. This approach is compatible with any object detector that utilizes a ReLU activation function. By applying a Gaussian noise layer to the network's final layers, BayesOD enables the calculation of both object space uncertainty and pixel space uncertainty for instance segmentation. We evaluate the framework's efficacy on state-of-the-art detectors, including Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, and YOLOv3, using the COCO dataset. Our results demonstrate that BayesOD accurately predicts both classification and localization uncertainty, achieving state-of-the-art performance in uncertainty estimation for deep object detectors. Furthermore, we show that these uncertainty metrics can be leveraged to enhance the performance of uncertainty-guided ensemble methods. We examine the interferometric Particle-Accelerated Light Generation (PANEL) scheme, which utilizes a laser-driven electron bunch to generate transversal modes within a vacuum. Our findings indicate that the bunch induces significant coupling between these modes, resulting in a photon distribution across multiple transversal channels. This distribution creates a pronounced deviation from the classical pigeonhole effect, thereby diminishing the nonlocality of the photon distribution. Consequently, we conclude that this reduced nonlocality renders the Bell inequality violation unobservable in the PANEL setup. Furthermore, we demonstrate that employing a pinhole to filter the transversal modes can restore the nonlocality, enabling the detection of a clear pigeonhole effect. Finally, we explore the potential of this approach to investigate foundational questions in quantum mechanics. These conclusions are supported by a detailed analysis of the photon probability distribution and the associated Wigner function. Additionally, we outline a feasible experimental protocol for implementing this proposal. Ultimately, our results offer a novel perspective on the foundational aspects of quantum mechanics and establish a new framework for interferometric particle acceleration. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into the quantum foundations of light generation. Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) have recently become a prominent area of research, yet their internal architecture remains largely opaque. This opacity complicates the understanding of how specific design choices impact performance and hinders the creation of new, high-performing DGNN models. This paper introduces a novel perspective on DGNN architecture design by examining the interaction between global and local topology link rewiring. We demonstrate that a DGNN model can be decomposed into two primary components: a global pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton and local topology link rewiring. We argue that optimizing both components is essential for achieving high performance. To validate this, we propose a new architecture design principle that prioritizes the pyramid-like skeleton first, followed by local rewiring. We present GPDSNet, a new model built upon this principle, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art DGNNs on four real-world datasets. We introduce a differentially private algorithm for low-rank matrix completion that utilizes the Huber mechanism. This approach involves estimating the matrix's underlying components and subsequently applying the Huber mechanism to release these estimates. We demonstrate that this method achieves an additive error of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nm}/\varepsilon)$ under $\varepsilon$-differential privacy. Furthermore, we establish that this error bound is optimal up to logarithmic factors for any differentially private algorithm addressing this problem. Finally, we empirically compare our proposed mechanism against two existing alternatives: the Gaussian mechanism and a recent algorithm by Balle et al. (2019). Our results indicate that the Gaussian mechanism performs poorly in this context, while both our method and that of Balle et al. (2019) outperform the Huber mechanism described therein. We introduce a unified model that describes the extinction, emission, and polarization properties of diffuse interstellar matter (ISM). This model relies on a single population of silicate grains and two distinct types of carbonaceous grains: amorphous carbon and aligned, thin, irregularly shaped dust grains (referred to as astrodust). The astrodust component is responsible for the polarization of starlight and the emission from aligned, polarized polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). We demonstrate that the Astrodust+PAH model accurately reproduces the wavelength-dependent extinction curves, the morphology of the 2175 \AA\ absorption feature, and the polarization of the extinction curve across the ultraviolet to near-infrared spectrum. Additionally, the model successfully accounts for the morphology of the polarization curve, the polarization fraction, and the polarization angle of dust emission in the far-infrared to submillimeter range. By combining the Astrodust+PAH model with the widely used Draine model, we show that the latter can be simplified to include only amorphous carbon grains. This reduction significantly lowers the number of free parameters in the Draine model, thereby enhancing its utility for analyzing observational data. We also examine the implications of this unified framework for interpreting the morphology of the 2175 \AA\ feature and the polarization of dust emission. Furthermore, we explore the potential for using the polarization of dust emission to investigate the shape and alignment of astrodust grains. Finally, we apply the Astrodust+PAH model to the diffuse ISM of the Milky Way and the Large Magellanic Cloud, demonstrating its ability to reproduce the observed wavelength-dependent extinction curves, polarization of the extinction curve, and polarization of dust emission. Our findings indicate that astrodust grains are more abundant in the Large Magellanic Cloud than in the Milky Way. We conclude that the Astrodust+PAH model offers a comprehensive description of the physical and geometrical characteristics of dust grains in the diffuse ISM. This model can be readily adapted to describe dust in other galaxies and the intergalactic medium. The model's parameters are accessible via a dedicated website. The Astrodust+PAH model is designed to be easily integrated into radiative transfer and polarization codes, enabling the calculation of extinction, emission, and polarization properties of dust in the diffuse ISM. We anticipate that this model will facilitate a more accurate analysis of observational data and a deeper understanding of the physical and geometrical properties of dust in the diffuse IS

We report the detection of a giant planet within the disk surrounding the very low-mass star CIDA 1, a system previously identified as a candidate for the lowest mass ratio between a primary and secondary object. By analyzing ALMA 1.3 mm continuum and CO isotopologue data, we identified a ring-like structure in the dust continuum emission, which we interpret as a gap carved by the planet. The planet is located at a semi-major axis of approximately 100 au, with an estimated mass of 1.5–2.5 Jupiter masses. This system represents the second known instance of a giant planet sculpting a disk around a very low-mass star, and it is the first such case where the planet is inferred from gas kinematics rather than directly imaged. The presence of this planet in the disk of a very low-mass star further complicates the understanding of the relationship between stellar and planetary masses. Additionally, we observed a large, bright dust ring at roughly 150 au, which we attribute to the snow line of water ice. The inner edge of this ring aligns with the snow line, suggesting that dust is trapped there by a pressure bump created by the planet. This configuration may facilitate the formation of a second generation of planets. The disk's age of approximately 1 Myr, derived from the star's mass and luminosity, indicates that this system is in a very early evolutionary stage. The early formation of a massive planet in a disk around a very low-mass star is a significant finding that challenges current planet formation theories. Finally, we discuss the implications of this discovery for the study of very low-mass stars and brown dwarfs. Abstract interpretation is a static analysis technique that operates through three primary phases: concretization, abstraction, and the fixpoint computation known as the widening-narrowing loop. This paper introduces a novel variant where the widening-narrowing loop is decoupled into separate phases for abstraction and concretization. We demonstrate that this new variant maintains the same computational complexity as the original while offering superior modularity. Furthermore, we illustrate its application in a case study involving the static analysis of C programs. This new approach facilitates the integration of advanced techniques from other program analysis methods, such as inter-procedural analysis, type analysis, and slicing, into static analysis tools. Additionally, it enables the combination of these methods with program synthesis, allowing for the construction of more precise abstract domains. The paper concludes by outlining several promising avenues for future research. We investigate the spontaneous excitation of a neutral atom and the resulting electromagnetic radiation emitted toward a thin mirror. By utilizing the Green function for a vacuum bounded by a thin, perfectly conducting sheet, we calculate these quantities for an atom initially in its ground state as a function of the sheet's thickness. Our findings indicate that the mirror triggers atomic motion, leading to both excitation and de-excitation. Furthermore, we observe that the probability of excitation can exceed that of a free atom, with the associated radiation exhibiting a complex spectrum. We also examine the implications of these results for an atom near a perfectly conducting sphere. Finally, we discuss how these conclusions extend to a dielectric sheet. These results are applicable to atoms in close proximity to a mirror, where the atomic transition wavelength is significantly larger than the mirror's thickness. Additionally, we explore the potential relevance of these findings to atoms in ultra-cold atomic gases situated near a thin mirror. In this context, the collective behavior of atoms facing the mirror could be substantial, with collective effects arising from dipole-dipole interactions between neighboring atoms. This scenario is particularly relevant when the interatomic distance is much smaller than the transition wavelength. This paper introduces a novel fairness metric for graph machine learning, termed "fairness with localized neighborhood fairness constraints" (FLN). FLN ensures that for any two nodes within a graph, if their respective neighborhoods are nearly identical, then their predicted labels must also be highly similar. We develop a unified optimization framework for FLN, enabling the simultaneous learning of both representations and classifiers. To address the non-convexity of this framework, we propose a two-stage algorithm: first, we derive a closed-form solution for the optimal graph representation, and second, we apply a Bregman divergence-based proximal gradient method to optimize the classifier. We demonstrate the efficacy of FLN across various graph classification tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and community detection. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of our proposed algorithm and its ability to recover the optimal solution of the FLN framework. Experimental results confirm the method's effectiveness in enhancing both the accuracy and fairness of graph machine learning. This study investigates supersymmetry (SUSY) within the final states characterized by jets and missing transverse momentum. The analysis utilizes data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, gathered by the CMS experiment at the LHC during 2016 and 2018, with an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. The search targets a natural SUSY framework where gluinos decay into final states featuring multiple jets and significant missing transverse momentum. Additionally, the study examines a split-SUSY scenario where gluinos are heavy and decouple, focusing on top quark pair production where each top quark decays into a jet and missing transverse momentum. No significant excess over the Standard Model background was observed. Consequently, 95% confidence level limits were established for natural SUSY models involving gluino masses up to 2.2 TeV, top quark pair production up to 1.1 TeV, and chargino masses up to 1.0 TeV. Furthermore, for the split-SUSY case, 95% confidence level limits were set for top quark pair production up to 1.1 TeV and neutralino masses up to 1.0 TeV. These constraints are applicable to a broad range of natural SUSY and split-SUSY models. The derived limits for chargino and neutralino masses are also relevant to searches conducted at $\sqrt{s} =$ 8 TeV and 13 TeV using final states with jets and missing transverse momentum. This study introduces a new econometric framework designed to identify rational expectation asset price bubbles. The proposed stochastic process incorporates a mean-reverting termination time, which fluctuates around a constant mean, alongside a jump-diffusion component. This model enables the application of the econometric bubble detection technique developed by Hamilton and Wu (2008) to isolate the bubble component within the asset price. We evaluate the model's performance using both Monte Carlo simulations and an empirical analysis of the S&P 500 index. The results indicate that the model can accurately detect bubbles and effectively replicate the observed features of the S&P 500. Furthermore, the proposed framework offers a more realistic representation of bubble dynamics compared to existing models in the literature. Specifically, it addresses the limitation of previous studies where bubbles were modeled as reverting to zero, a constraint that often conflicts with the rational expectations hypothesis. By allowing the bubble to revert to a positive mean, the model provides a more robust foundation for rational expectation bubble detection. Additionally, the model demonstrates the capacity to replicate the power law distribution of bubble durations, a feature that has historically posed significant challenges for researchers in this field. We conclude that the proposed approach offers a promising avenue for future research in the field of bubble detection. We investigate a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to a time-dependent driving force. By employing a Trotter decomposition, we transform the time evolution operator into a series of operators representing the undriven system, interspersed with Gaussian wave function updates that incorporate the effects of the time-varying external force. This decomposition enables a straightforward calculation of expectation values for arbitrary operators. We validate the method by computing the position and momentum distributions, as well as the Wigner function, for a coherent state. Additionally, we demonstrate the approach's utility in calculating the average position of a driven oscillator initialized in its ground state. Finally, we illustrate how the method can be applied to determine the fidelity of a driven oscillator prepared in its ground state. These findings indicate that the proposed technique is both efficient and versatile for analyzing the dynamics of driven quantum systems. Item recommendation systems are essential for enhancing user experience and driving the growth of online platforms. While recent research has leveraged sentiment analysis to improve these systems by integrating review data, current approaches often overlook the impact of temporal dynamics on sentiment opinions. Furthermore, existing methods fail to effectively capture the interplay between user behavior and sentiment expressions. To address these limitations, this paper introduces the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which employs a novel architecture for sentiment-informed item recommendation. SIFN utilizes a bidirectional recurrent neural network to model the temporal evolution of user behavior and sentiment reviews. It further incorporates a multi-layer attention mechanism to automatically identify and emphasize the most significant interactions between users and items. Finally, the model integrates multiple information sources to generate comprehensive feature representations for both users and items. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that SIFN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate that no subgroup of the homeomorphism group of a compact surface, which fixes the boundary and acts with sufficient transitivity on the interior, can be Roelcke precompact when equipped with the topology inherited from the compact-open topology. Consequently, this Roelcke precompactness property is not hereditary within the hierarchy of uniformities. Furthermore, the groups described are the sole non-compact surfaces whose homeomorphism groups (preserving the interior and fixing the boundary) admit a compatible left-invariant proper metric. The proof relies on the fact that the action of the described groups on the boundary is highly transitive, which in turn implies the existence of a sequence of homeomorphisms converging pointwise to the identity while exhibiting rapid growth on the diameters of their images. The argument is initially presented for the 2-sphere and subsequently extended to other compact surfaces through the use of quasi-isometries. A significant portion of the paper is dedicated to establishing the necessary background and definitions, as the inquiry into precompactness in the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets for surface homeomorphism groups appears to be unexplored. Additionally, the paper offers a concise overview of the theory of minimal dynamics on the shift space $2^{\mathbb{Z}}$. Finally, we outline a broader question regarding the precompactness of the centralizer of a homeomorphism within the group of all surface homeomorphisms. The examples provided in this context include the shift map on $2^{\mathbb{Z}}$ and the time-1 map of a geodesic flow on a negatively-curved compact surface. We conjecture that the described properties hold for the shift map and that they also apply to the time-1 map of a geodesic flow on a negatively-curved compact surface, provided the flow is not periodic. However, we note that the statement fails for the time-1 map of a geodesic flow on a negatively-curved compact surface if the flow is periodic. The examples illustrating this failure are the identity map and the time-1 map of a rotation on the 2-sphere. We anticipate that this result will be extended to other compact surfaces in future work. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings for the theory of amenable groups. We investigate integrable boundary conditions within generalized $\lambda$-deformations, demonstrating that they correspond to non-Abelian T-duals of bi-Yang-Baxter deformations. Specifically, we establish that the boundary conditions for the dual theory align with those of the original theory under specific constraints. Furthermore, we derive the effective worldsheet theory for the dual model associated with a group manifold, revealing that it retains the structure of a generalized $\lambda$-deformation. Finally, we present explicit examples of these integrable boundary conditions.

Our method successfully untangles every valid Hex mesh, including those with non-manifold boundaries, by performing at most 58 Tet removals per initial Tet.
