Relation extraction (RE) is a critical NLP task focused on identifying semantic relationships within text. While many RE approaches utilize pre-trained language models like BERT, they often depend on substantial annotated data. This study demonstrates that integrating knowledge graph link prediction can enhance RE performance. We introduce a unified framework that integrates link prediction and relation extraction into a single model, which can be fine-tuned using only relation extraction training data. This approach eliminates the need for additional training data regarding entities or their connections. Experimental results on the WebReasoning and RE data demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we show that the proposed framework can be effectively trained exclusively on WebReasoning data. Finally, we highlight the framework's ability to leverage external knowledge graphs, such as ConceptNet, to improve RE outcomes. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345678/LinkExp. Please cite the following paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04001.

This paper introduces a novel analytical delay model for CMOS inverters that leverages Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox to establish a continuous function linking inverter delay to load capacitance and input transition times. The methodology begins by simulating inverter behavior across a wide spectrum of input transition times and load capacitances using HSPICE. Subsequently, these simulation outcomes are utilized to derive the continuous delay function via the toolbox. The resulting model demonstrates high accuracy, with a maximum error of 2.5% relative to HSPICE data. Furthermore, the study compares this analytical approach to the widely adopted Elmore delay model, revealing that the latter fails to accurately predict inverter delay under certain conditions. The proposed model is also validated against experimental data obtained from fabricated inverters. Ultimately, this method offers a highly accurate delay estimation technique applicable to both discrete inverter chains and larger CMOS circuits. Additionally, the methodology is easily extensible to other logic gates and can be readily adapted for use in other SPICE simulators. The accompanying Matlab code is available for download at: https://github.com/abdelrahimhassan/CMOS_Inverter_Delay_Model.

Keywords: CMOS, Inverter, Delay Modeling, SPICE, Matlab, Curve Fitting Toolbox.

The ventral temporal cortex (VTC) is hypothesized to organize semantic categories along a continuum of animacy, ranging from animals to plants to artifacts. While this animacy gradient has been linked to the organization of visual object representations, the underlying mechanism driving this organization remains unclear. To address this, we examined the relationship between animacy and visual complexity using data from the CUB200 dataset, which includes 117 animal species. We quantified visual complexity using the entropy of the Fourier spectrum and assessed the correlation between animacy groups and complexity metrics. Our results indicate that visual complexity increases gradually as animacy decreases from animals to plants to artifacts. Furthermore, we trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict animacy categories from CUB200 images and analyzed the CNN's internal representations. We found that the CNN's feature representations align with our empirical findings, suggesting that the ventral temporal cortex may similarly organize visual inputs based on a complexity gradient. These findings support the hypothesis that the animacy organization in VTC is driven by a visual complexity gradient. Additionally, we explored the link between visual complexity and the visual cortex's ability to predict semantic categories, revealing that complexity correlates with the model's performance in predicting animacy groups. Finally, we demonstrated that the CNN's performance in predicting animacy categories improves as the number of visual layers increases. Collectively, these results suggest that the visual organization of the ventral temporal cortex is driven by a visual complexity gradient. This study offers a novel perspective on the animacy organization in VTC, providing new insights into the functional architecture of the human visual cortex. This study introduces a structure-preserving filter designed for multidimensional finite element simulations. The development of this filter relies on two key principles: first, the application of convex optimization to enhance simulation stability; second, the maintenance of critical structures within the finite element mesh, such as peaks, valleys, and ridges. The filter is constructed in two stages: initially, a structure-preserving convolution kernel is derived through convex optimization, followed by the design of a structure-preserving filter based on this kernel. The paper provides a detailed derivation of the filter and validates its effectiveness using various 2D and 3D finite element simulations. Results demonstrate that the proposed filter successfully maintains essential mesh structures and yields superior performance compared to the Gaussian filter. Furthermore, the filter exhibits robustness against noise and effectively preserves the geometry of the mesh. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/SPF. This study employs the broad-band Insight-HXMT to investigate the evolution of the corona in the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571, which is currently in the hard state. By analyzing type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) across the entire observation period, we tracked the evolution of their centroid frequencies and energy spectra. Our results indicate that the QPO centroid frequencies initially decreased and subsequently increased, while the spectral hardening index (HI) exhibited an inverse trend. Furthermore, we observed that the HI experienced a sharp decline during the transition from the hard to the intermediate state. These findings suggest that the corona in MAXI J1535-571 is not static but evolves dynamically, a behavior that may be common among black hole X-ray binaries. Additionally, the observed evolution of the QPO centroid frequency aligns with the predictions of the frequency-mass ratio relation. Finally, we propose that the observed evolution of the QPO centroid frequency can be interpreted as a manifestation of the changing position of the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). These results offer new insights into the nature of type-C QPOs and the dynamics of the corona within black hole X-ray binaries. This paper introduces a new approach to cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) that leverages the transferability of power functions. We propose a novel social intrinsic motivation (SIM) framework termed "transfer empowerment," which drives agents to generate actions that significantly boost their partners' performance. This concept offers a fresh perspective on how agents can develop a sense of agency regarding their partners through the empowerment of others. We demonstrate that transfer empowerment effectively induces a reliable sense of responsibility among agents, enabling them to react meaningfully to their partners' actions. Furthermore, we show that agents can acquire this sense of responsibility even when communicating only the value of empowerment rather than the full power function, proving that transfer empowerment is robust against the loss of information inherent in value-based learning. Finally, we validate that transfer empowerment successfully fosters a sense of responsibility in both continuous and discrete action spaces. Experimental results indicate that agents trained with transfer empowerment respond meaningfully to their partners' actions, whereas agents trained without this SIM fail to react to them. Additionally, we observe that incorporating transfer empowerment into the cooperative MARL algorithm substantially enhances the joint performance of the agents. Our findings suggest that transfer empowerment serves as a novel, effective, and computationally efficient method for developing a sense of responsibility in cooperative MARL. This paper examines the recent research on Lie 2-algebras, also known as strict Lie 2-algebras, with a focus on their connection to 2-vector spaces. We introduce the notion of a non-degenerate Lie 2-algebra and explore its associated concepts, including radical, ideal, and decomposability. Furthermore, we define abelian extensions of Lie 2-algebras and demonstrate that every such extension splits. The study subsequently addresses degenerate Lie 2-algebras, where the automorphism concept is generalized. We establish the existence of maximal and minimal subalgebras within Lie 2-algebras featuring a degenerate binary operation. Additionally, we investigate extensions involving 2-vector spaces and prove that any 2-vector space can be expressed as a direct sum of two subspaces, one of which is an ideal. Finally, we outline several research directions for future work. The paper concludes with an appendix providing illustrative examples. Unlike traditional approaches, our technique generates dense correspondences by leveraging global image context. This study examines the impact of measurement bias on data analysis within solar vector magnetic field observations. We identify the specific bias inherent in the Inferred Total Vector Signal (ITVS) method, which stems from the assumption that measurement errors are normally distributed. This assumption is flawed because systematic errors in solar vector magnetograms are inherently non-normal. Consequently, we demonstrate that the standard error in ITVS is overestimated, leading to an underestimation of bias in inferred measurements. To address this, we introduce a novel approach for calculating ITVS error that avoids reliance on normality assumptions. Furthermore, we propose a new technique for inferring line-of-sight (LOS) measurements from multi-pixel vector magnetograms that circumvents the normality assumption and the constraint that errors must be uncorrelated across different wavelengths. We illustrate the efficacy of these methods using data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). Our results indicate that the new ITVS method yields more accurate error estimates, while the new LOS inference method produces unbiased results with superior noise characteristics compared to the traditional approach. These findings are particularly significant for analyzing small-scale structures in the solar atmosphere, where noise can significantly influence outcomes. We conclude that these improved techniques are essential for future research in solar physics. Additionally, we have developed a Python package to facilitate the application of these methods, which is available on GitHub. Specifically, the results indicate that consumers can achieve up to a 10% reduction in costs compared to traditional DSM strategies. Additionally, we offer a novel perspective on the relationship between the continuous spectrum and weak mixing within ergodic theory. We introduce a novel approach for detecting metal-poor stars using the astrometric and photometric data from the Gaia Data Release 3 (Gaia DR3). This technique leverages the astrometric selection function, which favors stars with low metallicity, and analyzes the blue/visual color distribution to distinguish them from solar-metallicity stars. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through a test on the Gaia DR3 half-mission source list, where we identified 1,000 metal-poor stars with a mean probability exceeding 99.9% and a false positive rate below 0.01%. Furthermore, we developed a pipeline to automatically extract astrometric and photometric data from Gaia DR3, which is publicly accessible. This tool is particularly valuable for researchers aiming to expand the sample of known metal-poor stars. Our results indicate that the sample is highly homogeneous, with a mean probability of 99.9% and a false positive rate under 0.01%. The sample exhibits a broad range of [Fe/H] values spanning from -2.5 to -0.5, and we observe a correlation between the [Fe/H] and [M/H] values derived from the APOGEE and Gaia DR3 samples, respectively. This suggests that the [M/H] estimates from Gaia DR3 are reliable and can be utilized for future studies. We conclude that the sample of metal-poor stars identified in this work is robust and can serve as a valuable resource for the astronomical community. This study introduces a new dataset for predicting fire season severity, defined as the count of fires occurring during a specific period. We examine this time series data across 11 regions in the United States, covering both spatial and temporal dimensions. By analyzing the data, we identify key drivers of fire severity, including temperature, precipitation, and vegetation indices. Furthermore, we develop a forecasting model that integrates both statistical techniques and machine learning algorithms. The results demonstrate that combining these approaches yields superior performance compared to using either method alone. Finally, we provide an online application that utilizes our model to predict fire severity for the upcoming season. Our work offers a comprehensive framework for analyzing and predicting fire severity, with potential applications extending to other fire-affected areas globally. This study investigates the relationships among various corpus-derived metrics for morphological complexity. We evaluate seven syntagmatic measures and three brigaded measures, which include both syntagmatic and paradigmatic dimensions. By calculating correlations among these seven measures across a sample of 100 languages, we identify strong associations among most of them. Additionally, we propose a validation method that examines the relationship between language diversity and morphological complexity. Our results indicate that both syntagmatic and brigaded measures correlate positively with language diversity, though paradigmatic measures yield weaker correlations. We conclude that these measures capture distinct aspects of language, with paradigmatic measures reflecting the least amount of variation. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for cross-linguistic typology. (English)

Our analysis reveals that the abundance of these features is highly sensitive to the dark matter halo profile, which is governed by the strength of self-interactions. We find that the observed strong lensing rate aligns well with cold dark matter models, whereas the rate of weak lensing events in cluster centers is significantly lower than predictions from these same models. This discrepancy suggests that dark matter self-interactions may be substantial, with a cross-section of $\sigma/m \sim 1$ cm$^2$/g. This paper introduces M-ar-K-FastICA, a novel method for Independent Component Analysis (ICA) designed to efficiently identify source signals from mixtures using only second-order statistics. By integrating the moment-matching technique with K-FastICA, our approach extends the applicability of FastICA to problems involving non-Gaussian, non-negative, and non-symmetric sources. Furthermore, we show that the approach is computationally efficient, achieving a speedup of 10 to 100 times compared to the baseline K-FastICA algorithm. Finally, we highlight that M-ar-K-FastICA offers a significant advantage over existing methods by enabling the separation of non-negative sources from noisy mixtures. These findings underscore the method's potential for diverse applications, such as audio source separation, hyperspectral image analysis, and single-cell RNA sequencing. In display advertising auctions, publishers often face the challenge of determining bid amounts to maximize revenue while adhering to a specific budget. This paper introduces a new online learning framework designed to address this issue. The framework enables publishers to dynamically adjust their bids based on real-time feedback from the auction, ensuring their total spending remains within predefined limits. We propose an algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{T} + B)$, where $T$ represents the number of bidding rounds and $B$ denotes the magnitude of the budget constraint. This theoretical guarantee surpasses existing methods, which typically offer regret bounds of $O(\sqrt{T})$ that do not account for budget limitations. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical findings through extensive experiments using real-world data. These results demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of both revenue generation and computational efficiency. Wigner negativity and quantum steering are both recognized as indicators of non-classicality. While it is established that quantum steering implies Wigner negativity for single-qubit states, the relationship between these two concepts in higher-dimensional systems and multi-qubit composite systems remains unclear. This work investigates quantum correlations within higher-dimensional states and their connections to Wigner negativity. We demonstrate that unconditionally bounded quantum coherence is a necessary condition for Wigner negativity in symmetric qubit states. Furthermore, we show that both Wigner negativity and quantum coherence can be generated through local operations and classical communication (LOCC) when assisted by an ancillary system. Finally, we establish that Wigner negativity is not merely a consequence of quantum steering in multipartite systems; instead, we construct a family of multipartite Wigner-positive states that exhibit quantum steering. These findings offer new insights into the interplay between Wigner negativity and quantum steering. Additionally, we explore the relationship between quantum discord and Wigner negativity, revealing that Wigner negativity is not required for the presence of quantum discord. These results provide a foundation for exploring quantum resource theories involving Wigner negativity. Ultimately, our findings have significant implications for quantum information processing, particularly in the context of quantum error correction. Specifically, we show that Wigner negativity can be utilized to construct a set of non-orthogonal, Wigner-positive, mutually unbiased bases. This construction enables the design of a new class of stabilizer codes capable of correcting errors associated with these bases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such codes can detect and correct errors arising from quantum coherence and asymmetry. These contributions pave the way for advancing quantum error correction techniques. Finally, we examine the impact of Wigner negativity on quantum metrology, illustrating that the quantum Fisher information of Wigner-positive states can be enhanced through local operations and classical communication. These results highlight the potential of Wigner negativity in practical quantum applications. In quantum key distribution (QKD) systems utilizing privacy amplification, the random seed supplied by the user is typically assumed to be uniformly distributed. However, in practical scenarios, this assumption often fails because the seed is derived from a random number generator (RNG) that may produce non-uniform outputs due to inherent entropy sources. This deviation can compromise the security of the final key. This study addresses QKD security under conditions where the privacy amplification random source is non-uniform. We introduce a modified version of the bound analysis, demonstrating that the original analysis remains valid only when the statistical distance of the random source is sufficiently small. Our proposed bound analysis offers a more efficient approach for calculating the minimum two-way reconciliation information required to derive the final key. Furthermore, we validate the bound analysis through simulations of the BB84 protocol, confirming its accuracy. Finally, we apply this analysis to the decoy-state BB84 protocol, successfully calculating the secure bound analysis for both uniform and non-uniform random sources. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for the secure implementation of QKD with privacy amplification using non-uniform random seeds. Additionally, this work serves as a preliminary step toward developing QKD systems that rely on low-cost RNGs. This paper investigates the geometric characteristics of timelike Bertrand curves within the three-dimensional semi-Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}_3^1$. We demonstrate that for a pair of timelike Bertrand curves, the constant $a$ in the relation $\langle \mathbf{x}_1(s) - \mathbf{x}_2(\bar{s}(s)), \mathbf{t}_1(s) \rangle = a$ can assume the values $1$, $-1$, or any non-zero real number distinct from these two. Furthermore, we establish that if the torsion $\tau_1$ of a timelike Bertrand curve $\mathbf{x}_1(s)$ varies, then the constant $a$ must be either $1$ or $-1$. Additionally, we derive that the torsion $\tau_2$ of the corresponding partner curve $\mathbf{x}_2(s)$ satisfies the equation $\tau_2 = \frac{\tau_1}{1 - a\kappa_1 e \bar{s}'(s)}$, where $\kappa_1$ denotes the curvature of $\mathbf{x}_1(s)$ and $e \in \{1, -1\}$. Finally, we examine specific cases where $a = 1$ and $a = -1$. These findings generalize and extend previous research by A. Ali and M. A. Qureshi (2009) and A. Ali and M. A. Qureshi (2010). The study concludes with a classification of timelike Bertrand curves based on their geodesic curvature. Notably, this work represents the first systematic treatment of the case where $a = \pm 1$. The results are supported by illustrative figures and include a comprehensive bibliography of 40 references. We demonstrate that waveguide QED offers a versatile platform for investigating photon-photon interactions, with the strength and character of these interactions governed by the number of photons, the count of two-level atoms, and their respective positions. Leveraging these controlled interactions, we propose a method to generate arbitrary two-photon multi-mode entangled states. Furthermore, we illustrate how to construct multi-photon multi-atom entangled states by employing a diagrammatic approach to analyze photon scattering within waveguide QED systems. This technique involves calculating the probability amplitudes for incoming photons to scatter into various output modes and subsequently summing these amplitudes across all possible scattering configurations. We validate this proposed method by successfully generating diverse multi-photon multi-atom entangled states, including those involving three and four photons. Additionally, we introduce a novel two-photon two-atom state that cannot be achieved through simple coupling to waveguide modes. These findings are expected to facilitate the exploration of multi-photon multi-atom quantum phenomena and enable the creation of complex multi-photon multi-atom entangled states. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these states in quantum information processing. We investigate spin-dependent (SD) scattering for boosted dark matter (BDM), deriving the general SD cross section for a mediator with arbitrary spin. Our analysis reveals that SD interactions are amplified by a factor of $(m_\chi/v)^2$ compared to target-bound nucleons, where $m_\chi$ denotes the dark matter mass and $v$ represents the velocity of the dark matter-nucleon system in the dark matter rest frame. This enhancement is particularly pronounced for BDM, where $v$ is significantly lower than in the standard halo case. Consequently, despite the reduced phase space available, BDM retains a scattering cross section that is orders of magnitude larger than that of halo nucleons. We demonstrate that this effect can be observed in existing data from the LHC and the IceCube experiment. Furthermore, we show that for boosted dark matter, spin-independent scattering is further boosted by a factor of $(E_\chi/m_\chi)^2$ relative to the non-relativistic regime, where $E_\chi$ is the dark matter energy. This leads to an even greater increase in the cross section, making BDM interactions potentially orders of magnitude stronger than SD interactions in the non-relativistic case. These findings underscore the critical role of boosted dark matter in constraining dark matter mediators. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for future searches. Our findings indicate that the current lack of detection of mediators with spin-dependent couplings to nucleons may stem from the fact that SD scattering is significantly stronger for boosted dark matter. Therefore, future searches must account for the possibility that mediators are being missed due to their interactions with boosted dark matter. We conclude by outlining prospects for detecting BDM, emphasizing the need for a multi-messenger approach that leverages both collider and astrophysical data. Specifically, we propose that a combination of LHC and IceCube data could enable the detection of a 100 GeV dark matter candidate with a coupling strength of $10^{-28} \, \mathrm{cm}^2$. This represents an improvement of several orders of magnitude over current bounds derived from non-relativistic data. Additionally, we highlight the potential of future colliders to detect dark matter with a mass up to approximately 10 TeV. Such a discovery would necessitate a thorough investigation into the associated astrophysical signals. This paper introduces a delay optimization technique for the conventional non-coherent differential detection of continuous phase modulation (CPM). By leveraging the inherent memory of differentially detected CPM signals, the method reduces the number of differential detection branches required in traditional detectors. When applied to a binary 4-PSK signal, this approach cuts the required branch count by half, thereby lowering computational complexity and power usage. Furthermore, the method is compatible with existing CPM transmitters and can be implemented via a simple software update. We analyze the spectral statistics of random band matrices deformed by a complex symmetric matrix of finite rank. The unperturbed parent ensemble, which interpolates between the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) and the Wigner-Dyson semi-circular law, consists of symmetric real matrices with independent entries possessing a finite variance that scales with the matrix dimension $N$. The deformation is characterized by a complex coupling constant $\lambda$ and a rank $k$ that remains small relative to $N$. We demonstrate that the spectral statistics of this deformed ensemble are well-described by the Gaussian $\beta$-symmetric sigma-model, where the symmetry class is determined by the complex nature of the coupling. This finding extends the earlier result by Erdős, Yau, and Yin, which addressed the case of a single rank deformation. Furthermore, we establish that the spectral statistics remain independent of the rank $k$ and the specific variance profile of the parent ensemble, provided the variance scales appropriately with $N$. The validity of this approximation holds for both the large $N$ limit and a regime where the coupling constant $\lambda$ is sufficiently small. Our methodology relies on the local semicircle law and the fundamental gap estimate for the Dyson-Schwinger equations. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for the variance of the linear statistics of eigenvalues, showing that it scales with $N$ and converges to the variance observed in the Gaussian $\beta$-ensembles. This result is achieved by demonstrating that the variance of linear statistics for the deformed band matrix can be bounded using the variance of linear statistics for Gaussian matrices, which in turn is controlled by the fundamental gap of the corresponding differential operator. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending these findings to other parent ensembles, such as the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. The paper concludes with a discussion of open questions. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical component of machine learning, yet it remains difficult to quantify. This paper introduces a framework based on human learning to measure algorithmic interpretability, corresponding to a cognitive complexity score. The framework posits that algorithmic interpretability reflects the learning process humans employ to understand machine learning models. We demonstrate that this framework aligns with established definitions of algorithmic interpretability and can be efficiently computed. Furthermore, we apply this framework to evaluate the interpretability of decision trees, linear models, and logistic regression, with experimental results validating our approach. To our knowledge, this work represents the first attempt to define algorithmic interpretability through the lens of human learning. This paper introduces a reparameterisation of the standard log-location-scale model for extreme value data, which is defined by three parameters: a Poisson process rate, a scale parameter, and a threshold. We demonstrate that this new formulation possesses a more favourable geometry, thereby enhancing the performance of standard Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. A Bayesian case study involving annual maxima of daily rainfall in Adelaide, Australia, is used to validate these claims. Furthermore, we illustrate that this reparameterisation enables the straightforward construction of a non-parametric estimator for the underlying rate function. Finally, we show that a Bayesian inference approach utilizing this reparameterisation can effectively model extremes within a non-stationary framework. The proposed methods are implemented in the R package {\tt extPOIS}. All code required to replicate the numerical examples is made available as a supplementary file. We present the results of a spectroscopic study on 10 red giant branch (RGB) stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808, utilizing the UVES spectrograph at the ESO VLT. Our analysis yielded high-precision radial velocities and elemental abundances for carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sodium, magnesium, aluminum, silicon, calcium, and iron. The derived iron abundances average to [Fe/H] = -0.80 ± 0.05, aligning with prior studies. However, we identified a significant spread in iron content among the stars, with a dispersion of $\sigma_{[Fe/H]} = 0.12$ dex. This variation is statistically significant at the 3.5$\sigma$ level and confirms the presence of multiple stellar populations within the cluster. Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between the abundance of $\alpha$-elements (O, Mg, Si, Ca) and iron, indicating a shared origin for these elements. The observed abundance patterns are consistent with those produced by the $\alpha$-process in massive stars. Additionally, we detected a significant correlation between the abundance of odd-Z elements (C, N, Na, Al) and iron, which suggests a common origin for these elements as well. The correlation between sodium and aluminum is particularly notable, as it is typically attributed to the Na-O-Ne cycle in massive stars. These findings support the hypothesis that the multiple populations in NGC 2808 arose from the mixing of material from the cluster's birth cloud. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the formation mechanisms of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters. Single file systems serve as a fundamental model for investigating constrained diffusion. In this study, we analytically derive the full first exit time statistics for a chain of $N$ particles confined within a finite box, assuming nearest neighbor interactions and hard core repulsion. We demonstrate that these exit time statistics are primarily driven by the system's entropy, which manifests as an entropic barrier to diffusion. By employing an effective single particle approach, we derive the complete exit time statistics for a classical Brownian particle subject to this entropic barrier. Furthermore, we examine the impact of the system size on these exit time statistics. Our findings indicate that while the system size does not alter the general characteristics of the exit time statistics, it does influence the mean exit time. Specifically, the mean exit time for the entire system scales as $N^3$ in the limit of large $N$. This scaling behavior is consistent with the mean first passage time of a Brownian particle across an entropic barrier, which also follows an $N^3$ dependence. Finally, we compare our theoretical results with molecular dynamics simulations. The close agreement between our theoretical predictions and the simulation data confirms the validity of our approach. These results provide valuable insights into the exit time statistics of single file diffusion and offer a robust theoretical framework for analyzing this phenomenon. This apparatus demonstrates the ability to measure transmission with a precision of 1% across the 200–300 nm spectrum. Image retrieval is a critical challenge in modern information retrieval, particularly for users seeking to locate images related to their work or daily lives. While active image retrieval has been explored in various contexts, this paper introduces a novel approach called active image indexing. Unlike traditional methods, our system allows users to interact with images during retrieval, enabling them to provide additional information about a target image to guide the search. We have developed a proof-of-concept implementation that supports users in attaching text, images, or drawings to a retrieved image. The system then uses this attached content to find new images sharing the same identifier. Furthermore, we have created a dataset of images annotated with their IDs to evaluate the system's performance. Experimental results demonstrate that active image indexing can significantly improve retrieval performance. Finally, we outline potential future research directions for this work. The code is accessible at https://github.com/andreasgk/active-image-indexing.

This paper investigates keyless authentication for point-to-point communication over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels. In this framework, a transmitter and receiver exchange messages over a noisy channel without a pre-shared secret key, relying instead on public discussion and random channel inputs to generate a shared key. We examine two distinct keyless authentication schemes: one utilizing public discussion exclusively, and another combining public discussion with random channel inputs. For both schemes, we analyze the trade-off between key rate and authentication rate. Our findings indicate that for a fixed key rate, the public discussion-based approach achieves a higher authentication rate when the channel is sufficiently noisy. Conversely, when channel inputs are permitted, the public discussion-based approach yields a lower required key rate for any given authentication rate, provided the channel is not too noisy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for both schemes, the achievable region is convex, allowing for the application of time-sharing strategies. Finally, we derive the fundamental limits of key rate and authentication rate for both schemes, along with their respective trade-off curves. Numerical results are provided to illustrate these limits and compare the performance of the two schemes. Additionally, we explore the asymptotic behavior of these regions as the channel becomes increasingly noisy, revealing that the region for the scheme with channel inputs converges to that of the public discussion-only scheme in the limit of infinite noise. We investigate the dynamics of a Brownian particle moving along a periodic potential under constant force and thermal noise. In the regime of weak, white noise, the particle exhibits a net drift that scales linearly with the noise intensity. We derive the analytical expression for the correction to this linear response, demonstrating that it follows a quadratic scaling at very low noise levels. Furthermore, we show that this correction can unexpectedly cause the drift velocity to decrease as noise intensity increases. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Our results are applicable to various systems, including charge transport in periodic superconducting structures and the motion of colloidal particles within optical lattices. Additionally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for the broader field of dispersionless transport. Finally, we highlight the potential for observing these effects in the context of molecular motors. This paper introduces a flexible local projection method designed to estimate impulse responses to various shocks. The approach utilizes a set of flexible projection functions to model the conditional mean of a specific time horizon's outcome following an event. We demonstrate that the asymptotic normality of the estimator for the event time's parameter holds true. This normality allows for the construction of confidence intervals for impulse responses at any horizon, while accounting for estimation errors in the event time's parameter ensures valid inference. Furthermore, we develop a finite-sample correction to enhance the accuracy of the confidence intervals. A simulation study confirms the method's performance, and an application analyzes the impact of monetary policy shocks on U.S. industrial production. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions of the proposed framework. The code required to replicate the results is available at https://github.com/SebastianKuehn/LocalProjections. Fine-grained named entity typing (FGET) involves classifying entities into specific subtypes within a predefined taxonomy. This task is particularly challenging due to the vast number of subtypes in certain domains and the significant overlap between them. To address this, we introduce a novel approach leveraging the geometric properties of hyperbolic space. This method capitalizes on hyperbolic space's ability to accommodate exponentially increasing subtypes within a confined area and its inherent hierarchical structure. By embedding subtypes into a hyperbolic space that preserves their hierarchy, we can more effectively differentiate between similar categories. We present two refinement strategies to enhance the model's performance: the Type Embedding Refinement (TER) method, which adjusts type embeddings to better represent the hyperbolic structure, and the Hyperbolic Self-Supervised Learning (HSSL) method, which utilizes synthetic data to strengthen subtyping distinctions. Experimental results across three FGET tasks demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. This paper examines functions belonging to the class $\mathcal{U}$, defined as those where the imaginary part of $z f'(z)$ lies within the unit disk for all $z$ in the unit disk. The study establishes sharp upper bounds for the second Hankel determinant of $\mathcal{U}$, denoted $H_{2,2}(z,f)$, and identifies the extreme functions. Additionally, we derive sharp bounds for $H_{2,2}(z,f)$ for the general class of univalent functions $\mathcal{S}$. Finally, numerical examples are provided to validate the findings. The results indicate that the maximum value of $|H_{2,2}(z,f)|$ for functions in $\mathcal{U}$ is significantly lower than that for the general class $\mathcal{S}$. Furthermore, the bound for $\mathcal{U}$ is shown to be sharp, achieved by the extreme function $u(z)=\frac{1+z}{1-z}$. In contrast, for the general class $\mathcal{S}$, the bound is not sharp. These findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of the second Hankel determinant for both $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{S}$. The techniques employed are also applicable to other significant classes of univalent functions. This research contributes to the broader field of geometric function theory and its applications in complex analysis. This study introduces a novel load-balancing strategy for prepartitioning virtual machines (VMs) within a cloud data center. The primary objective is to minimize energy consumption by reducing the total number of active physical machines (PMs) required to host the VMs. The proposed prepartition algorithm addresses two key challenges: (1) assigning incoming VMs to specific PMs, and (2) migrating VMs from overloaded PMs to underutilized ones. To tackle the first challenge, the algorithm evaluates the impact of each PM's configuration on overall power usage and selects an optimal setup. For the second challenge, it identifies overloaded PMs and strategically migrates their hosted VMs to less loaded PMs. Performance was assessed using a real-world cloud dataset, and the prepartition algorithm was benchmarked against the state-of-the-art repartition algorithm. Results demonstrate that the prepartition algorithm reduces the count of active PMs by 10% compared to the repartition algorithm. Furthermore, it achieves a 20% reduction in active PMs relative to a naive prepartition approach. Finally, the prepartition algorithm successfully handles a four-fold increase in VM arrival rates without compromising performance. We introduce a new framework for equilibrium prediction in games, termed Fixed Point Networks (FPTN). This approach leverages the observation that Nash equilibria can be defined as fixed points of a best-response mapping. FPTN employs a neural network to approximate this mapping and identifies its fixed points to forecast equilibria. We demonstrate that FPTN can be efficiently trained using only best-response data from a limited number of game profiles, without requiring direct equilibrium samples. Furthermore, we establish that FPTN can precisely predict equilibria for specific game classes, such as piece-wise linear games, and show that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we present empirical evidence indicating that FPTN effectively generalizes to predict equilibria in games beyond those seen during training. This work addresses the problem of bounding causal effects in the presence of unmeasured confounding. Initially, we derive bounds on causal effects using only assumptions regarding the sign of the confounding influence. Subsequently, we extend these findings to high-dimensional settings where numerous covariates are observed. By leveraging the sparsity of the causal graph, we demonstrate that these bounds can be tightened. Finally, we apply these results to estimate the causal impact of air pollution on human health. Our analysis utilizes a high-dimensional causal graph derived from a large-scale meta-analysis involving over 100,000 individuals. We show that the proposed bounds yield significantly narrower estimates for the causal effect of air pollution on respiratory and cardiovascular diseases compared to conventional methods. This paper introduces a new predictive monitoring framework designed to identify stealthy attacks on linear time-invariant systems. Unlike conventional methods that rely on residual analysis, this proposed approach leverages the system's inherent dynamics to detect attacks. The study addresses two distinct monitoring strategies: one for systems with known system matrices and another for systems where these matrices are unknown. In both scenarios, the authors formulate the monitoring problem as a convex optimization task. Furthermore, they introduce a novel prediction-based attack detection scheme utilizing the Entropic-SOS hierarchy, demonstrating that this scheme can be efficiently solved via semidefinite programming. Finally, the effectiveness of these predictive monitoring schemes is validated through numerical simulations. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. The primary contributions of this work are threefold: (i) the development of predictive monitoring schemes for linear time-invariant systems, applicable to both cases with known and unknown system matrices; (ii) the formulation of these schemes as convex optimization problems; and (iii) the extension of these schemes to handle systems with unknown system matrices. The proposed approach is applicable to a broad range of linear time-invariant systems. Text summarization remains a highly active area of research, with recent deep learning approaches achieving state-of-the-art results. However, most current models are tailored for English and lack generalizability to other languages. This paper introduces GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised graph-based framework designed for Indian languages. The model constructs a graph from input sentences using a pre-trained multilingual language model, generating sentence representations that are fed into a graph attention network. This architecture enables the model to identify and aggregate relevant sentences within the graph. Experimental results across three Indian languages demonstrate that GAE-ISumm effectively summarizes various domains, including news, movie reviews, and social media posts. This paper introduces a novel deep learning-based quantization method for Gray-coded modulation, designed to approximate the sigmoid function and enable the transmission of calculated L-values. The approach utilizes a single fully connected layer with a sigmoid activation function to model the relationship between input and output values. The proposed scheme is evaluated using 16-QAM and 64-QAM modulations. Simulation results demonstrate that the method achieves a significant reduction in Bit Error Rate (BER) performance degradation compared to existing techniques. Additionally, the study examines the impact of noise and channel impairments on the system's BER. Finally, the computational complexity of the proposed solution is analyzed. The paper concludes that the method is highly efficient for practical implementation. This study examines the complexity of the UPWARD PLANARITY problem, which involves determining whether a directed acyclic graph can be drawn in the plane such that all edges follow the direction of their source and target vertices. While the general UPWARD PLANARITY problem is NP-complete, we demonstrate that it admits a parameterized algorithm with runtime $O^*(2^k)$ when parameterized by the number of vertices of degree 3. Furthermore, we establish that UPWARD PLANARITY is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the size of the largest subdivision of a claw. Finally, we address the problem of counting the number of upward planar drawings for a given directed acyclic graph, proving that this counting problem is also NP-hard. However, we show that it can be solved in $O^*(3^k)$ time when parameterized by the number of degree 3 vertices. Additionally, we illustrate that the problem of counting upward planar drawings is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the number of vertices with in-degree and out-degree both equal to 2. Our findings are based on a novel characterization of upward planar drawings. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first parameterized algorithm for UPWARD PLANARITY and the first exploration of counting upward planar drawings. The proposed algorithms are straightforward and efficient, with a runtime of $O^*(2^k)$ for the algorithmic problem and $O^*(3^k)$ for the counting problem, where $k$ denotes the number of degree 3 vertices. These methods are also applicable to the more constrained variants of UPWARD PLANARITY known as RIGID UPWARD PLANARITY and STRAIGHT-EDGE RIGID UPWARD PLANARITY. In both cases, the number of solutions is either 0 or 1, and the number of vertices with degree exceeding 3 is bounded by the number of degree 3 vertices. Consequently, our algorithms yield a polynomial-time solution for RIGID UPWARD PLANARITY and STRAIGHT-EDGE RIGID UPWARD PLANARITY, with a running time of $O^*(2^k)$. Notably, the straight-edge variant of RIGID UPWARD PLANARITY is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the number of degree 3 vertices. We also consider the general case of UPWARD PLANARITY, where edges are not required to be straight, and show that it can be solved in $O^*(3^k)$ time

Crowdsourced datasets are frequently employed to generate training data for machine learning models, yet they often suffer from noise due to the involvement of multiple human annotators. This study examines the efficacy of ensemble modeling in mitigating such noise within specific annotator groups. We introduce a novel ensemble method that surpasses existing techniques by assigning distinct weights to each annotator group based on their individual performance. Additionally, we propose a new metric for measuring uncertainty in class labels, termed "Human Softmax," which quantifies the probability distribution over classes for a specific training example as inferred from the annotators. This metric enables the identification of training examples where annotator opinions diverge, thereby highlighting the presence of noise. We evaluate our approach using a classification model trained on a crowdsourced dataset of movie reviews, demonstrating that our method enhances classification accuracy compared to baseline approaches. Furthermore, we show that the Human Softmax metric effectively captures the degree of uncertainty in the assigned labels. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the advantages and limitations of our approach. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Ensemble-Modeling-for-Noisy-Crowdsourced-Datasets.

We demonstrate exponential decay in the Hölder norm for transfer operators acting on smooth observables within uniformly and nonuniformly expanding semiflows that exhibit exponential decay of correlations. These findings extend prior results, which were limited to flows, to the broader context of semiflows. Furthermore, we generalize the requirements by eliminating the need for spectral gap or polynomial decay of correlations assumptions. Our methodology relies on a recent advancement by Baladi and Todd regarding the cohomological smoothing of transfer operators. Additionally, we establish novel results for nonuniformly expanding flows and semiflows that are not necessarily Anosov. As an application, we derive new insights concerning the statistical behavior of geodesic flows on negatively curved manifolds. Specifically, for manifolds that are not compact, we prove the existence of exponential decay of correlations for Anosov flows and exponential decay of correlations for nonAnosov semiflows that are conformally expanding. The latter result represents the first instance of such a finding for a semiflow that is not a time-one map of a volume-preserving flow. Our approach also yields results for conformally expanding semiflows that are not Anosov, thereby generalizing the work of Demers and Liverani. Finally, we prove the existence of a Markov partition for conformally expanding semiflows that are not Anosov, extending Demers' findings. In the specific case of geodesic flows on negatively curved manifolds, this constitutes the first such existence proof for a semiflow that is not a time-one map of a volume-preserving flow. Additionally, we establish the existence of a Markov partition for geodesic flows on compact manifolds featuring cusps, a result that had previously been unproven. Our methodology is applicable to various classes of semiflows beyond those related to negatively curved manifolds. We also introduce a framework for analyzing transfer operators on Banach spaces of functions defined on the stable manifolds of a semiflow, which may find utility in other areas. Finally, we present a general theorem regarding the regularity of eigenfunctions for transfer operators associated with semiflows, which can be applied to derive regularity results for transfer operators on negatively curved manifolds. A strength-$t$ covering array, denoted as $\mathrm{CA}(N,t,k,q)$, is an $N \times k$ matrix with entries from a $q$-ary alphabet, where every $N \times t$ submatrix includes each of the $q^t$ possible $q$-ary $t$-tuples a $\lambda$ multiple number of times. The covering array number $\mathrm{CA}(N,t,k,q)$ represents the minimum row count $N$ for such an array. This study examines covering arrays of strength 2 with 3 columns over a binary alphabet, specifically those achieving the optimal $\mathrm{CA}(N,2,3,2)$ row count. We demonstrate that any such covering array can be decomposed into a union of two specific types of arrays, designated as type 1 and type 2. Furthermore, we establish that for $N \ge 10$, no type 2 array exists within any optimal covering array. These structural findings are utilized to derive several lower bounds for $\mathrm{CA}(N,2,3,2)$. Additionally, we present a straightforward algorithm to construct optimal strength-2 covering arrays with 3 columns over a binary alphabet for all $N \le 100$. Finally, we offer a conjecture regarding the existence of type 2 arrays for $N \ge 100$. The paper concludes with a computational complexity analysis of the problem. We demonstrate that if Alice and Bob utilize a noisy maximally entangled state in a nonlocal game, the game's value can be approximated to any desired precision through repeated executions and post-processing of the outcomes. This resolves an issue raised by Brandao, Yuen, and Watrous (2016) and establishes a significant advancement over prior research. Specifically, our approach is significantly more straightforward than the recent undecidability proof by Guha, Jain, and Upadhyay (2020), which addresses games allowing access to an arbitrary number of copies of the state. Furthermore, our method yields a substantial improvement upon the QMA(2)-completeness result established by Brandao, Yuen, and Watrous (2016). By integrating the techniques from both lines of work, we prove that for any nonlocal game employing noisy maximally entangled states, the value lies within QMA(2), thereby confirming the inclusion $\text{MAX-EPR} \subseteq \text{QMA(2)}$. Additionally, we establish that these problems are complete for a new complexity class, $\text{EPR}$, which we introduce. This class encompasses problems where the verifier possesses the ability to query the player's state with an arbitrary unitary transformation. Our findings indicate that $\text{EPR}$ occupies a position strictly between QMA(2) and EPRC, as it is contained within both of these established classes. Finally, we explore the properties of the $\text{EPR}$ class and propose a conjecture regarding its characterization. Notably, we demonstrate that the EPR class remains closed under complementation only when the number of qubits is fixed. This leads to the intriguing possibility that the hierarchy of EPR classes does not collapse at any finite level, thereby providing evidence that the undecidability result by Guha, Jain, and Upadhyay (2020) extends to the EPR class. Furthermore, we establish that the EPR classes are contained within PP, a result that relies on a novel technique for bounding the trace distance between two density matrices. This technique may hold independent interest. Our work also offers a partial explanation for the discrepancy between the QMA(2)-completeness of MAX-EPR and the undecidability of certain related problems. This study aims to replicate the results of a previous paper using the same methodology. The original paper's code is unavailable, so we have developed our own genetic algorithm implementation. Our primary objective is to demonstrate that a non-trivial automated crash reproduction system can be built using a guided genetic algorithm. Consequently, this work validates that approach without needing to address specific enhancements or refinements to the method. Although this is merely a partial reproduction, it successfully confirms the effectiveness of the guided genetic algorithm for automated crash reproduction. The findings suggest that future research should focus on the method's specific improvements and optimizations. Ultimately, this effort contributes to the broader goal of minimizing manual effort in crash reproduction. The accompanying document provides a detailed analysis of the reproduction process, while the included video demonstrates the algorithm's execution. All necessary data and source files are available in the repository. We hope this work is as useful to you as it has been to us. Your feedback and suggestions would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.

The phase diagram of high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductors includes a pseudogap phase above the superconducting critical temperature $T_\textrm{c}$, where various theories propose that this phase consists of a distinct vortex lattice. This study presents neutron diffraction findings from underdoped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.67}$, revealing that vortices form a square lattice at low temperatures and transition to a fourfold symmetric but distorted square lattice at elevated temperatures. This observation supports the hypothesis that the pseudogap phase comprises a unique vortex lattice. Furthermore, the observed transition temperature aligns with the pseudogap crossover temperature identified in other experiments. These results suggest that the vortex lattice within the pseudogap phase exhibits greater stability than previously thought. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the vortex lattice persists in the pseudogap phase even when superconductivity is suppressed by magnetic fields. Finally, the findings indicate that the vortex lattice in the pseudogap phase is more robust than the pseudogap itself. These conclusions are derived from measurements conducted in magnetic fields oriented both parallel and perpendicular to the crystal's $c$-axis. The data are interpreted using a model where vortices interact via anisotropic elastic forces and the repulsion arising from the pseudogap phase. This model successfully explains the observed lattice distortions and the stability of the vortex lattice within the pseudogap phase. Furthermore, the study confirms that the vortex lattice in the pseudogap phase is stabilized by the superconducting condensate, even when its density is significantly lower than that of the vortex lattice at $T_\textrm{c}$. This study examines the ground states of two-dimensional (2D) triangular and kagome lattices featuring nearest-neighbor (NN) and next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) interactions. We demonstrate that for NN interactions, the ground state is always a 12-sublattice ferromagnetic (FM) order, regardless of whether interactions are ferromagnetic (FM) or antiferromagnetic (AFM). For NNN interactions, we identify two distinct regimes: a weak-interaction region where the ground state is a 6-sublattice ferrimagnetic (FIM) order, and a strong-interaction region characterized by a 12-sublattice ferrimagnetic (FIM) order. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of a uniform external magnetic field on these systems. Finally, we outline the phase diagrams for both NN and NNN cases. These findings may offer valuable insights into the magnetic behaviors of various triangular and kagome lattice materials. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive list of all possible magnetic orders in these 2D structures. This work could assist in classifying the magnetic orders of diverse triangular and kagome materials. To facilitate this classification, we have also developed a user-friendly computational tool. The source code for this tool is publicly accessible via a GitHub repository. We anticipate that these tools will be valuable for researchers studying triangular and kagome materials. In large-scale experiments, researchers frequently face the challenge of identifying a subset of units that exhibit distinct treatment effects. While the literature has extensively addressed this issue under independence assumptions, dependence structures remain a significant concern. This study introduces a novel method for multiple hypothesis testing under dependence to detect units with non-null treatment effects. The approach is grounded in the concept of False Discovery Rate (FDR) control within subgraph-based local dependence frameworks. We demonstrate that the proposed FDR procedure maintains error rate control and achieves substantial gains in statistical power. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm to calculate FDR-adjusted $p$-values for testing treatment effects. Extensive simulations and two real-world case studies confirm the method's favorable performance in terms of error rate control and statistical power. The p-values generated by our procedure are accessible via an online repository. Additionally, the procedure's code is available in the R package "TeFD" (Treatment Effect FDR Detection). This work extends our prior research, which was published in the *Journal of the American Statistical Association* (2022). The current manuscript incorporates several enhancements, including a more rigorous theoretical analysis, a new fully adaptive procedure, and the integration of covariate information. This article examines the fundamental principles of the standard cosmological inflation model, which addresses the flatness and horizon problems inherent in the Big Bang framework. It further explores the initial conditions and potential energy functions required to initiate inflation, as well as the mechanisms that terminate it. The text also covers how inflation can generate density fluctuations that evolve into the observed large-scale structure of the universe, with a specific focus on the prediction of nearly scale-invariant fluctuations. Additionally, it briefly touches upon the theory of chaotic inflation and its connection to string theory. Finally, the article examines the critical issue of the cosmological constant and outlines various alternative theories of inflation. Throughout, it emphasizes the profound impact inflation has had on particle physics and cosmology, including the elucidation of the universe's flatness and the prediction of gravitational waves. The discussion concludes with an analysis of the current observational status of the theory. This material is intended for advanced undergraduate and graduate students in physics. This paper examines the viability of the type-X two-Higgs doublet model (2HDM) as a potential solution to both the $W$ mass and muon $g-2$ anomalies. We identify the region of parameter space capable of resolving these puzzles and find that, while solutions exist, they are constrained to a narrow range. Furthermore, we analyze the phenomenological implications of these allowed regions, with a specific focus on the decay of the lightest CP-even scalar into a pair of lightest CP-odd scalars. Our findings indicate that this specific decay channel could offer a promising avenue for detecting new physics at the High-Luminosity LHC. Additionally, we explore the prospects for discovering the additional scalars within the viable parameter space at future electron-positron colliders. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the muon $g-2$ experimental outcomes at the Fermilab Muon $g-2$ project. In conclusion, the type-X 2HDM offers a viable framework to address both the muon $g-2$ and $W$ mass anomalies. This would necessitate a broader investigation into the phenomenology of such models. When developers receive a new requirement, they often need to determine the current state of the system to decide on an implementation approach. A common initial step involves checking if the concept already exists within the codebase. Concept location tools assist in this process by highlighting the most relevant source code elements, such as classes, methods, or fields. However, developers frequently struggle to formulate effective queries for these tools, leading to a high rate of discarded queries. This paper introduces QUICKAR, a technique that automatically generates multiple query reformulations by leveraging crowdsourced knowledge. By utilizing a large dataset of concept definitions and their corresponding usage instances from various projects, QUICKAR automatically constructs a graph representation of concept usage. This graph is then queried to extract reformulations, which are subsequently evaluated for quality using a novel metric called "relevance." Experimental results demonstrate that QUICKAR can automatically produce high-quality reformulations, with an average of 1.5 useful suggestions per query. Furthermore, an empirical study involving 12 professional developers confirms that these automatically generated reformulations are perceived as useful. QUICKAR is designed to be adaptable for use with any concept location tool. The source code for QUICKAR is accessible at https://github.com/quickar/quickar. QUICKAR is anticipated to be released as an open-source tool to facilitate further research and development. We introduce a suite of open-source web-based tools designed for the visualization and analysis of spectral data, with a specific focus on the characterization of exoplanets and their atmospheres. This functionality is accessible via the open-source platform Reflectance and Spectral Data Explorer version 2 (RCSEDv2; https://rcsed2.org/). The tools support both interactive and static visualization of spectra, enabling users to examine individual spectral features and their associated physical parameters. Additionally, they facilitate the analysis of spectral features by comparing observed spectra against theoretical models. The application's source code is hosted on GitHub (https://github.com/RCSED/RCSEDv2). RCSEDv2 is an updated iteration of the original application, which was developed to support the educational outreach initiative Spectroscopy for Kids. This new version incorporates several enhancements, including a more intuitive user interface, a more efficient architecture, and a suite of new tools for analyzing spectral features. The application is built using JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3, ensuring it is platform-independent and capable of running on any web browser. Furthermore, it is designed to be easily extensible, allowing for the addition of new spectral models and features. This paper outlines the features of RCSEDv2 and provides a tutorial on how to utilize the application. We anticipate that RCSEDv2 will be a valuable resource for both educational and research purposes. Using the current algebra framework, we investigate the production and decay of hidden-charm pentaquark states. In this approach, the baryonic component of the pentaquark is represented by the corresponding three-quark diatronic state, while the mesonic component arises from the quark-antiquark pair within the meson. We calculate the production amplitude for the pentaquark in the reaction $B+P\to P'+X$, where $B$ is a baryon, $P$ is a proton, and $P'$ and $X$ are the final-state proton and pentaquark, respectively. Furthermore, we derive the decay amplitude for the pentaquark via the process $P'\to B+P$. Our findings indicate that the production and decay of the pentaquark $P$ are linked by the relation $\mathcal{M}(B+P\to P'+X) = -\frac{\mathcal{M}(P\to B+P')}{m_P^2-m_{P'}^2}$, where $m_P$, $m_{P'}$, and $m_B$ denote the masses of the pentaquark, final-state pentaquark, and baryon, respectively. This relation holds for both vector and pseudoscalar pentaquarks. We also examine the implications of this relation for the production and decay of vector pentaquarks. Finally, we compare our results with experimental data on the production and decay of the pentaquark $P$. This study examines the impact of two feedback types—traditional detailed feedback and inquiry-based conceptual feedback—on software testing education. Through a within-subjects experiment involving 129 participants, we evaluated how each feedback mechanism influences student performance, effort, and satisfaction. The results indicate that inquiry-based conceptual feedback yields superior learning outcomes compared to traditional detailed feedback. Furthermore, we developed a framework for integrating this approach into software testing education and have made it available on GitHub. Our goal is to encourage the research community to explore the efficacy of inquiry-based conceptual feedback across various educational contexts. Domain adaptation is a widely adopted strategy for addressing the scarcity of labeled data in real-world applications. However, recent advancements in domain adaptation are largely confined to centralized environments where both source and target data reside on a single device. This paper introduces a decentralized domain adaptation approach that operates without access to source data, a scenario that is more practical for many applications. To achieve this, we propose a novel method that leverages hypotheses from unlabeled data to guide learning on a neighbor's domain-shifted unlabeled data. Specifically, we employ a hypothesis transfer mechanism to propagate these hypotheses across devices, thereby eliminating the need for model parameter sharing. We validate the efficacy of our approach across three tasks: cross-domain text classification, cross-domain graph classification, and cross-domain node classification. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be seamlessly integrated with various state-of-the-art algorithms without incurring additional computational costs. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Semi-Supervised-Hypothesis-Transfer. Finally, we hope this work inspires further research into decentralized domain adaptation. This study introduces a domain-informed neural network architecture designed for the task of object interaction localization. The approach is evaluated using simulated data from the DarkSide-50 experiment, a direct dark matter detection initiative. The model's efficacy is benchmarked against two baseline methods: a fully connected network and a point-based network. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed domain-informed network surpasses both baselines in terms of localizing interaction coordinates and identifying the corresponding detector planes. Furthermore, we establish a novel loss function tailored for this localization challenge, which facilitates more effective model training. Finally, we analyze the model's performance relative to the uncertainty inherent in the simulated data. These findings hold significant relevance for the broader field of object interaction localization, with potential applications extending to astroparticle physics, medical imaging, and industrial vision systems. Atmospheric retrievals for exoplanets and brown dwarfs are becoming increasingly sophisticated, yet they face significant hurdles due to the scarcity of comprehensive molecular cross-section data. This study introduces EXOPLINES, a database of molecular line lists and cross sections tailored for the retrieval of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres. EXOPLINES incorporates line lists for 12 key molecules—H2O, CO, CO2, CH4, NH3, HCN, H2S, SO2, TiO, VO, CrH, and FeH—utilizing the HITRAN, ExoMol, and Hamann et al. (2014) data. Additionally, we provide HITRAN-based cross sections for N2, He, and H2. We have also expanded the HITRAN H2O line list to include lines up to the 10th vibrational band, enhancing the accuracy of H2O retrievals. Furthermore, we have expanded the ExoMol He line list to cover a broader temperature range. The EXOPLINES database is accessible via the Exoplanet Retrieval and Analysis Environment (EXORE), available at http://exo.re. The code is open-source, allowing users to easily add new molecules to the retrieval process. We demonstrate the database's utility by retrieving the atmosphere of the hot Jupiter HD 209458b, which aligns with prior studies. We also present retrievals for the hot Jupiter WASP-12b and the hot Saturn HD 80606b, both of which yield results consistent with existing literature. Finally, we illustrate retrievals for the brown dwarfs WISE 1828+0642 and 2MASS J0523-3657, confirming agreement with previous studies. EXORE is designed to be user-friendly and accessible to both professional and amateur astronomers. We anticipate that EXORE will facilitate the analysis of a wide array of exoplanets and brown dwarfs, thereby advancing the field of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheric research. EXORE is freely available for download at http://exo.re. We encourage the exoplanet and brown dwarf community to utilize EXORE for their research endeavors. We are committed to maintaining and expanding the EXOPLINES database to include additional molecules, isotopologues, and isotopic variants. This work examines and extends the use of grounding within Answer Set Programming (ASP) through the lens of model theoretic semantics. We demonstrate that standard ASP groundings are essentially initial segments of the universal grounding, which encompasses the ASP-program's classical and stable models. Furthermore, we explore various forms of partial grounding and establish that their combined application can generate any instance derived from applying an ASP-program to a specific model. These findings offer a novel perspective on grounding that accommodates practical variations found in ASP solvers. Additionally, our results provide a robust framework for addressing the issue of infinite groundings. Ultimately, this study offers a model theoretic foundation for grounding that unifies classical and non-classical interpretations. The paper includes several technical contributions to the fields of logic and ASP, such as a revised definition of immediate consequences for non-classical semantics, a new characterization of immediate consequences for Fuzzy Logic, and the introduction of the concept of "weakly monotonic" logics. These concepts are particularly valuable for grounding applications involving non-classical semantics. The study concludes with an outline of several open research questions. Notably, we address the challenge of determining whether a given instance of an ASP-program originates from a particular model, and we propose a solution to this problem. Finally, we present a series of open problems concerning the relationship between ASP groundings and classical or non-classical semantics. Quantum resource theory offers a systematic framework for investigating quantum resources, such as entanglement and coherence. This paper extends the second law of thermodynamics to broad quantum resources within any specific resource theory. We establish conditions for a quantum monotone applicable to both closed and open systems under certain constraints. These findings generalize previous research on the second law across various thermodynamic scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dual monotone of an asymptotic reversible quantum resource corresponds to the second law within that theory. Finally, we derive several applications of these results in the context of coherence theory. Consequently, this research provides a fundamental basis for future investigations into quantum resources. Additionally, it introduces a method for constructing quantum monotones in arbitrary resource theories, a tool that is highly valuable for quantum information processing. This work introduces a framework for quantifying information within complex systems using moment data. We define the information moment as the product of information entropy and the mean value, demonstrating its effectiveness in measuring information across various distributions, including uniform, Gaussian, and power-law. Furthermore, we establish a link between information and the moment spectrum, revealing that the index of this spectrum corresponds to the power-law exponent in scale-free networks. These proposed metrics are also applicable to modeling the evolution of information in complex systems. Finally, we illustrate the utility of these methods by analyzing the information content of the COVID-19 pandemic. This study investigates the bulk-boundary correspondence in disordered higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs) by analyzing the mobility gap and the stability of localized boundary states. The analysis reveals that the bulk-boundary correspondence fails in HOTIs, a result derived from the mobility gap's sensitivity to disorder. Furthermore, the coexistence of mobility gap and bulk gap is essential for the existence of localized boundary states. Finally, the impact of contact between samples on the mobility gap is examined, demonstrating that this effect can be mitigated by increasing the system size. These findings are applicable to both bosonic and fermionic systems. Additionally, the methodology is utilized to examine the bulk-boundary correspondence in disordered bosonic systems, specifically focusing on the bulk-boson-boson correspondence. The results indicate that the boson-boson correspondence is more fragile than the boson-bulk correspondence. Finally, the study explores the implications of these findings for the stability of edge and corner states in bosonic HOTIs. This research was conducted using the open-source Python package HOTIpy. The Python code and supplementary data required to reproduce the results are available at https://github.com/Hotipy/bulk-boundary-correspondence. We introduce Light Field Neural Rendering (LFNR), a method designed to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view light field recordings. Unlike conventional neural rendering techniques that rely on RGB images, LFNR utilizes complex-valued complex angular spectrum (CAS) plane representations. This approach enables the efficient encoding of both intensity and phase data, thereby preserving critical depth cues. By employing a neural network to learn the underlying physics of light propagation, LFNR can render novel views from any position within the scene. We demonstrate that LFNR achieves state-of-the-art performance in both quantitative and qualitative metrics for light field reconstruction. Furthermore, we show that a single LFNR model can be applied to reconstruct light fields from diverse cameras with varying focal lengths and sensor dimensions. Additionally, we highlight the model's ability to recover high-frequency details, such as sharp edges and fine textures, which are often lost in other neural rendering methods. Finally, we illustrate how these capabilities facilitate the generation of new depth maps. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1234/LFNR.
