We introduce a universal formula for finite-size corrections to wavefunction overlaps, valid for systems in the 2D conformal field theory (CFT) regime. This expression enables the precise determination of scaling dimensions for fused operators by analyzing wavefunction overlaps on finite lattices. The validity of the formula is confirmed across two distinct scenarios: first, within the generalized Lieb-Liniger model, where it accurately predicts previously unknown scaling dimensions; and second, in the numerically exact solution of the critical Ising-Haagerup model, where it facilitates the identification of scaling dimensions for operators emerging from the fusion of two primary operators. This latter capability is particularly valuable for higher-dimensional CFTs, where operator content is significantly more complex. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the finite-size correction term in our formula can be derived from the logarithmic term in the entanglement entropy of a single interval. This result offers a novel perspective on the relationship between entanglement entropy and the universal structure of wavefunction overlaps. Finally, we outline a systematic approach for extending these findings to other critical lattice models. This framework involves identifying the relevant operator content, computing the logarithmic coefficient in the entanglement entropy, and utilizing these elements to construct a universal finite-size correction formula. We anticipate that this method will facilitate the discovery of new scaling dimensions in critical lattice models that are inaccessible through standard techniques. Additionally, we derive a universal finite-size correction for overlaps involving operators with non-zero spin. This correction is essential for accurately describing the scaling behavior of the ground state overlap in spinor field theories, such as the 2D fermionic Hubbard model. Our findings suggest that this correction may also play a crucial role in the finite-size scaling of wavefunction overlaps in higher-dimensional field theories. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that the logarithmic coefficient in the entanglement entropy of a single interval in 3D CFTs is non-zero. Consequently, we propose that this coefficient could be significant for the universal finite-size corrections of the ground state overlap in various spinor field theories. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending these results to interacting field theories. We demonstrate that the logarithmic coefficient in the entanglement entropy of a single interval in 3D can be calculated using the conformal bootstrap method. This suggests that the associated finite-size correction in wavefunction overlaps could be determined within the framework of the conformal bootstrap. This finding is particularly promising for the study of interacting field theories, as it provides a new avenue for investigating the universal properties of operator content.

Part-of-speech (POS) tagging serves as a fundamental step for numerous natural language processing (NLP) applications. However, contemporary POS taggers, which are typically trained on modern texts, often yield unreliable results when applied to historical corpora. This paper introduces a new algorithm for handling POS tagging as an interval-valued prediction task. By utilizing a neural network, the algorithm generates an interval-valued prediction for each word, which is subsequently converted into a standard POS label. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art interval-valued classification techniques. Furthermore, the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in POS tagging historical corpora, specifically Old English and Early Modern English. The algorithm is implemented in both Python and C++. A technical report detailing the algorithm and its implementation is accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.00100. The source code can be found at https://github.com/andreas-kroher/interval-tagger. Additionally, a demonstration video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2222222222. Quantum error mitigation (QEM) methods are essential for obtaining reliable results on near-term quantum hardware. These findings indicate that the method is highly promising for mitigating noise in practical quantum computations. In a regular category, the direct image of a preorder along a functor fully preserving finite limits and colimits is generally not a preorder. However, if a sufficient condition is met, there exists a reflective subcategory where the image is fully closed; the reflector is the left adjoint to the inclusion, and its unit is fully universal. This subcategory comprises all objects possessing the required property, with preorders serving as the morphisms. We demonstrate that this sufficient condition holds for any topos and any locally connected category equipped with pullbacks. Furthermore, we establish that an equivalence relation is fully cocartesian (meaning its image is an equivalence relation) if and only if it is closed under diagonal relations. Finally, we characterize fully cocartesian preorders and equivalence relations within extensive categories that possess pullbacks. These characterizations involve universally initial relations and are valid in any such category. Additionally, we provide an example illustrating that a fully cocartesian preorder need not be a preorder within an arbitrary regular category. The paper concludes with several open questions. This study introduces a new spatial multivariate extreme value model designed for extreme events in the ocean. The methodology involves fitting univariate extreme value distributions to conditional extremes derived from a spatial window around each location. This process is repeated across all locations to generate a multivariate extreme value distribution that captures local dependencies. This study introduces a novel operator shifting technique designed to enhance the efficiency of iterative methods when addressing noisy linear systems involving non-Hermitian, potentially ill-conditioned matrices. The core strategy involves applying a polynomial filter to the standard iterative process, which relocates the majority of the residual to a higher frequency subspace that is subsequently eliminated via shifting. We establish the optimality of this approach regarding convergence rates relative to the matrix condition number and noise level, demonstrating that the method remains effective even when eigenvalues are situated near the imaginary axis. Furthermore, we develop a practical implementation utilizing Chebyshev polynomials and validate the theoretical findings through numerical experiments. The paper concludes by outlining potential applications within the fields of machine learning and quantum computing.

**Keywords:** Linear systems, iterative methods, operator shifting, polynomial filtering, quantum machine learning.

The metal-insulator transition (MIT) in V$_2$O$_3$ is driven by strong electron-electron interactions, a phenomenon that is significantly altered in ultrathin films. This study employs density functional theory (DFT) combined with DFT+DMFT to investigate the MIT in V$_2$O$_3$ films, specifically examining how the metal-insulator gap varies with different surface terminations. Our findings indicate that the insulating gap is most pronounced in a single unit cell and diminishes as the number of unit cells increases. Furthermore, the metal-insulator energy gap is highly sensitive to the specific atomic species present at the surface. These results offer valuable insights into the tunability of the MIT in transition metal oxides and establish a foundation for developing correlated materials for advanced electronic applications. Additionally, the methodology used is broadly applicable to a wide range of transition metal oxides. The accompanying data and code are accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10050001. This paper introduces a new class of control systems designed to steer specific conservation laws toward a desired target state. The study establishes the local well-posedness of this system around an equilibrium and demonstrates that the solution converges to a translated version of the target as time approaches infinity. These findings extend the work of Chen, Chen, and Zhang, who previously addressed the heat equation. Furthermore, the derived estimates are sufficiently robust to enable the application of similar techniques to other conservation laws. The analysis begins by defining the compressible Navier-Stokes equations as a conservation law and formulating an appropriate control problem. Subsequently, the paper proves the existence and uniqueness of local-in-time solutions, followed by an estimate that ensures the solution remains close to the target state. Finally, the convergence of the solution to the target is established. The methodology employed integrates techniques from reference [1] with those from this work. Additionally, the authors intend to explore applications for other conservation laws in future research. Non-performing loans (NPLs) represent a significant challenge for the banking sector, as they indicate a failure to generate expected revenue and impose substantial costs related to recovery and restructuring. Consequently, accurately identifying NPLs is crucial for banks to mitigate losses and enhance profitability. This study examines the predictive capabilities of various machine learning models using a dataset from a Tunisian bank. We evaluated eight models—Random Forest, XGBoost, AdaBoost, KNN, SVM, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, and Decision Tree—across three feature sets: initial, updated, and combined. The analysis revealed that the Random Forest model achieved the highest accuracy of 99.1% when utilizing the combined feature set. Furthermore, feature importance analysis indicated that the maturity rate, debt-to-asset ratio, and interest rate were the most predictive variables for NPL classification. These findings offer valuable insights for bank managers, enabling them to develop more effective early warning systems for NPLs. By leveraging these models, banks can improve their ability to forecast potential NPLs, thereby reducing associated losses and strengthening their financial resilience. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that machine learning offers a robust solution for NPL classification, providing a practical framework for banks to implement predictive systems. The dataset and code used in this study are accessible at: https://github.com/AmrElshenawy/NPL-Analysis. Future work will explore advanced machine learning techniques to further refine these predictive models. Additionally, we aim to apply these methods to other banks to validate the generalizability of our results. Finally, we plan to investigate the impact of external factors, such as economic conditions, on the performance of these models. This investigation will be conducted through time series analysis to assess how economic fluctuations affect the models' efficacy. By examining these factors, we aim to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges banks face in managing NPLs and the potential of machine learning to address them. This analysis will also help identify areas for model improvement and guide future research in this field. Ultimately, this approach will contribute to the development of more robust and reliable NPL classification systems. Furthermore, we intend to examine the performance of these models across different economic cycles to assess their stability and reliability in varying economic environments. This analysis will also help identify potential biases or limitations in the models, allowing for their refinement and optimization. By considering these factors, we can ensure that machine learning models continue to play a pivotal role in NPL classification, ultimately benefiting both banks and the broader economy. Finally

This paper introduces a new convolutional network layer designed to perform image recognition by convolving images with orientation-aware filters. Unlike standard convolutional layers, which are limited to translation equivariance, our proposed layer extends this property to include rotation, reflection, and scale. We provide a formal definition of orientation-aware filters and demonstrate that these filters can be represented as a sequence of such filters. Furthermore, we prove that a convolutional layer utilizing these filters achieves invariance to translation, rotation, reflection, and scale. Experimental results indicate that this new layer outperforms traditional convolutional layers in recognizing objects under the specified orientation transformations. Additionally, we show that the layer maintains robustness against orientation transformations even when training data is restricted to a single orientation. We name this proposed layer an Orientation Convolutional Network (OCN) and provide a PyTorch implementation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ocn-net/ocn. Our implementation also supports orientation transformations beyond those explicitly mentioned, such as shearing and perspective warping. This work investigates how the top quark mass depends on light, massive quark flavors. Utilizing the massive renormalization group equations for the QCD beta function and gamma_5 quark anomalous dimension, we derive an analytical expression for the one-loop strong coupling constant's dependence on heavy quark masses. Furthermore, we establish an exact relationship between renormalization schemes that differ in their treatment of the gamma_5 quark anomalous dimension. Applying these findings, we determine the relationship between the top quark pole mass and the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass at two-loop order, incorporating the masses of all quarks heavier than the strange quark. We also provide a two-loop expression for the quark flavor independence of the QCD strong coupling constant, which includes dependence on all quark flavors heavier than the strange quark in the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ scheme. Additionally, we present a two-loop expression for the quark flavor independence of the QCD strong coupling constant, where the heavy quark mass dependence is expressed in the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ scheme. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the quark flavor dependence of the top quark mass. Our findings indicate that the quark flavor dependence of the top quark mass is approximately 10% of the quark mass itself, with an uncertainty of about 1%. This dependence is primarily driven by gluon corrections to the quark self-energy, which are sensitive to quark masses, and by the massive quark contribution to the one-loop massive QCD beta function. We also examine the impact of the two-loop massive quark contribution to the QCD beta function. Our results suggest that the massive quark contribution to the two-loop beta function is negligible, as it is suppressed by the ratio of the massive quark mass to the renormalization scale. Consequently, the two-loop expression for the quark flavor dependence of the top quark mass can be accurately approximated by retaining only the one-loop contribution. This allows for a significant simplification of the two-loop expression for the quark flavor dependence of the top quark mass. We also explore the implications of these findings for the quark flavor dependence of the strong coupling constant. Our results suggest that the quark flavor dependence of the strong coupling constant is approximately 10% of the quark mass, with an uncertainty of about 1%. This dependence arises mainly from the massive quark contribution to the one-loop beta function

A vertex $v$ in an undirected graph $G$ is defined as almost regular if the absolute difference between the degrees of any two vertices, including $v$, does not exceed 1. This paper establishes that every connected almost regular graph $G$ possessing at least one regular vertex $v$ admits a $k$-coloring of its edges such that the set of colors incident to $v$ encompasses all $k$ colors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this result is optimal. Additionally, we derive several corollaries and conjectures based on our primary findings. Finally, we present computational evidence supporting these results for small graphs. The study concludes with a discussion of open problems. This work is a joint effort with J. Fiala, M. R. This study examines the spatial distribution of space debris in low Earth orbit (LEO) and its evolution over time. Utilizing a simplified model for debris evolution, we demonstrate that the steady-state density profile is governed by the ratio of atmospheric drag forces to collisional forces. We further show that the density profile's shape remains independent of the specific debris evolution model, provided the model adheres to a power-law relationship between debris mass and orbital lifetime. Additionally, we explore how the density profile is influenced by the power-law exponent. Finally, we outline the potential for extending this approach to more complex scenarios. These findings are supported by a low-complexity model of debris evolution, which is made available as open-source software. This software can be utilized to investigate the spatial distribution of debris in LEO and its temporal dynamics. Furthermore, the model is applicable to other celestial bodies, such as the Moon, and can be adapted to examine the distribution of debris in higher orbits. The research was conducted using the open-source Python package `space_debris_density`, which is accessible at https://github.com/astro-geodynamics/space_debris_density. The package includes a demonstration notebook that replicates the analysis presented in this paper. The system employs a new integer linear programming formulation to optimize the meshing process. Furthermore, we show that our approach can successfully create quad meshes for a selected set of open-source benchmark models. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/quadmesh. This paper derives formulas for the expected values and variances of sample correlation coefficients across all possible data permutations, expressed as functions of the underlying bivariate data distribution's first four moments. These formulas are generated using the symbolic computation software Maple. The study also examines the behavior of these moments when considering the expected value and variance of sample correlation coefficients under data permutations via randomization tests. Furthermore, the analytic formulas are applied to determine these quantities for specific distributions, including the bivariate normal, bivariate Student's t, and bivariate Laplace distributions. The derived expressions are utilized to construct confidence intervals for the expected value of the sample correlation coefficient across all permutations. Finally, the paper addresses the problem of testing the null hypothesis that the expected value of the sample correlation coefficient is zero across all permutations, with applications to the bivariate normal, bivariate Student's t, and bivariate Laplace distributions. Additionally, the results are applied to a real-world dataset comprising the daily closing prices of the S&P 500 and S&P 600 indices from January 2, 2000, to December 31, 2020. The paper concludes with a discussion of the findings. This derivation relies on the bootstrap principle, which demands that all three-particle amplitudes involving the scalar field be equivalent to those in free theory. We further generalize this approach to arbitrary spin fields and backgrounds, ultimately proposing that general gravity can be constructed via the same procedure. In this framework, the Einstein-Hilbert action emerges as the unique bootstrap-compatible action for a massless spin-2 field in a flat background. Finally, we explore the extension of this approach to higher-spin fields. In this scenario, the resulting actions resemble those of higher-derivative theories, yet they avoid the associated ghosts because the amplitudes remain those of a free theory. These actions are non-local, and we suggest that their non-locality is essential for bootstrap compliance. We also examine the construction of non-local actions for interacting spin-2 fields, where the amplitudes match those of general gravity, and discuss the implications of this finding. The growing popularity of recommendation systems has spurred significant research into their interpretability. While recent studies have evaluated various techniques for generating local post-hoc explanations, they have largely overlooked the quality of these explanations when they are inherently multidimensional. This paper introduces adherence and constancy as two novel metrics for assessing the quality of local post-hoc explanations in recsys. Adherence measures the degree to which an explanation aligns with the original recommendation model, while constancy evaluates the degree to which an explanation remains consistent across different models. We demonstrate the utility of these metrics by applying them to two common forms of local post-hoc explanations: perturbation-based and surrogate model explanations. Our results indicate that both explanation types exhibit high adherence to the recommendation model, though they differ in their constancy levels. Furthermore, we show that these constancy variations can significantly influence the quality of counterfactual feedback. To our knowledge, this is the first study to establish adherence and constancy as metrics for local post-hoc explanation quality. We have made our code and data accessible at https://github.com/alexandros-kap/evaluation-of-explanations-for-recsys.

The fast Sinkhorn algorithm serves as a widely adopted numerical approach for solving optimal transport problems involving two probability distributions of size $n$. Its primary benefit lies in achieving a computational complexity of $O(n^2 L)$, where $L$ denotes the desired number of iterations for convergence. This paper introduces a novel variant of the fast Sinkhorn algorithm designed to reduce the computational burden to $O(nL)$. The proposed method relies on a specific structure observed in a significant subset of optimal transport problems, characterized by a collinearity condition. We demonstrate that this condition allows for a substantial decrease in matrix inversion costs, transforming the operation from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. Furthermore, we present a new algorithm that leverages this insight to further lower the complexity to $O(n)$. Our findings indicate that the proposed method is highly effective for a broad range of problems, delivering substantial speed improvements over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, we illustrate its utility in a practical application: estimating the divergence between two sets of images. The experimental results confirm that the algorithm achieves a significant reduction in computation time compared to current solutions. The young, active M-dwarf AU Microscopii (AU Mic) hosts two confirmed planets, b and c. This study presents Far Ultraviolet (FUV) observations of AU Mic using the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) to investigate the star's high-energy radiation output and its potential impact on the atmospheres of its planets. By analyzing the FUSE spectrum, we identified 12 flares with a mean energy of 1.1 x 10^30 erg, occurring at a rate of 0.003 flares per second. The cumulative flare frequency distribution follows a power law with a slope of -0.77, a value consistent with other M-dwarfs. We calculated the total high-energy flux (XUV) from AU Mic, finding it to be 1.1 x 10^(-4) erg s^(-1) cm^(-2) at 0.02 AU and 1.3 x 10^(-6) erg s^(-1) cm^(-2) at 0.06 AU, corresponding to the orbital distances of planets b and c, respectively. These values represent 1.5% and 0.02% of the Sun's total XUV flux. Furthermore, we determined the photoevaporation mass loss rates for both planets, which are 1.5 x 10^10 g s^(-1) for planet b and 1.2 x 10^9 g s^(-1) for planet c. These rates are comparable to those observed in other exoplanets. Finally, we examined the photochemistry of H2O and CO2 in the atmospheres of AU Mic b and c, finding that the photochemical lifetimes of these molecules are significantly shorter than their dynamical timescales. This suggests that the atmospheres of both planets are likely in a steady state, with photochemistry occurring on timescales shorter than their dynamical timescales. The results of this study will inform future observations of AU Mic and its planetary system. (Abridged)

We introduce a novel model for radiation reaction friction, an effective force that scales with the fourth power of velocity ($v^4$) at non-relativistic speeds and approaches $v$ in the relativistic regime. This model is derived from the interaction between an accelerating charge and a Drude material medium, which is characterized by free carriers and localized oscillators. The resulting radiation reaction friction force exhibits a smooth, monotonic increase with velocity, accompanied by a corresponding radiation power emission. Furthermore, this power can be modulated by the material medium through the mixing of Debye and Lorentz forces. Finally, we apply this model to analyze the dynamics of a particle moving through such a medium. The particle's equation of motion reveals that its behavior can be either damped or anti-damped, depending on the specific properties of the medium. Additionally, we examine the steady-state motion of the particle under the influence of both Debye and Lorentz forces alongside radiation reaction friction, demonstrating that a stable solution exists under these combined conditions. Our findings indicate that radiation reaction friction offers a viable mechanism for energy dissipation within resistive material media. These results may have significant implications for understanding the dynamics of charged particles in various material environments, including solids, liquids, and gases. Potential applications span diverse fields, such as particle accelerators, space exploration, and particle physics. In classification tasks involving severely imbalanced datasets, standard nearest neighbor methods often yield poor results because the majority class dominates the decision boundary. This paper introduces a statistical approach designed to construct a refined training set that enhances the accuracy of nearest neighbor classifiers. The proposed method relies on estimating the conditional mean of the features given the class label. We provide a theoretical analysis of the relationship between the error rates of these classifiers and the bias within the estimated training set, demonstrating that the bias can be quantified using the divergence between the training and testing sets. Leveraging these insights, we develop a statistical framework to generate a training set with a specific bias parameter. We validate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and a real-world data analysis. The empirical findings indicate that the proposed method significantly improves classification accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algorithm is computationally efficient, with a time complexity of $O(n^2)$, where $n$ represents the number of training samples. We present a method for detecting charge tunneling events between a quantum dot and a superconducting island by utilizing gate sensing. This approach is applicable to systems designed to investigate Majorana bound states within the context of spin-charge conversion. By analyzing the dynamics of gate sensing, we derive the tunneling rate, which exhibits strong dependence on both temperature and detuning. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the measured signal is primarily driven by spin-polarized tunneling. These results offer a valuable tool for characterizing tunneling processes in systems intended for topological qubit implementation. Additionally, we demonstrate that this technique can be extended to measure the exchange coupling between two quantum dots. Our findings are validated using a realistic model of a triple-dot system. We present a theoretical framework describing the Rayleigh-plateau instability in a liquid coating on a solid cylinder, where surface tension drives the breakup of the film into droplets. Our model accounts for the finite thickness of the liquid layer and axial viscous drag from the surrounding medium, represented as a function of the cylinder's rotation rate. We derive the most unstable wavelength and its associated growth rate, demonstrating that rotation can significantly amplify both the instability growth rate and the wavelength. Furthermore, we show that the critical Weber number—the threshold at which rotation suppresses instability—varies with rotation speed and film thickness, reaching a maximum at an optimal rotation rate. Finally, we validate our theoretical predictions using high-speed imaging experiments. These findings are pertinent to various industrial applications involving liquid coatings, such as wire and fiber coating, paint application, and food processing. Additionally, our results offer insights into the behavior of liquid films in natural settings, including atmospheric aerosols and biological systems like blood vessels and plant xylem. Ultimately, this model provides a foundation for understanding the formation of liquid droplets on cylindrical substrates. This paper investigates the time-dependent Lipschitz stability of $\alpha$-dissipative solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation, where $\alpha \in [0,1]$. We demonstrate that for any two such solutions, the $L^\infty$ norm of their difference remains bounded by a constant multiple of their initial discrepancy. This finding represents the first establishment of Lipschitz stability for the equation, marking a significant advancement toward proving well-posedness. Furthermore, our result confirms the stability of recent constructions of non-uniqueness solutions, thereby clarifying the relationship between uniqueness and stability in this context. Finally, we outline an extension of these results to a broader class of dissipative equations. Notably, the primary findings are derived through an elementary method that relies on the equation's structure rather than variational principles. Consequently, this approach yields a direct proof of the uniform bound on the difference of two solutions within the energy space, a result that has recently been utilized to construct solutions exhibiting $\omega$-nonuniqueness. Additionally, this work provides the first instance of $\alpha$-dissipative solutions being shown to be stable under perturbations. Finally, we present a counterexample illustrating that the Lipschitz stability of the Hunter-Saxton equation cannot be derived from the Lipschitz stability of the Camassa-Holm equation. These results collectively offer a comprehensive understanding of the stability properties of the Hunter-Saxton equation. As a byproduct, we establish the well-posedness of the equation in the space $H^1(\mathbb{R})$. The paper concludes with an outline of the proof strategy for the Hunter-Saxton equation, which also applies to the more general $\alpha$-Camassa-Holm equation. This work is a joint effort with J. **Background:** The increasing adoption of robotic ultrasound scanners in clinical settings has sparked a need to evaluate their reliability compared to traditional manual techniques. This study aimed to assess the consistency of measurements derived from both robotic and manual ultrasound scans of the spine in pediatric scoliosis patients.

**Methods:** A total of 10 scoliosis patients underwent ultrasound scanning of their thoracic and lumbar spines using three distinct approaches: two independent sonographers using manual scanners and one independent operator using a robotic scanner. The primary metrics recorded were the T5-L5 vertebral body height ratio (VHR) and the T5-L5 vertebral body angle (VBA). These measurements were analyzed using intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) to determine reliability.

**Results:** The analysis revealed that robotic scanning yielded highly reliable VHR and VBA results for both the thoracic and lumbar regions, with ICC values exceeding 0.90. In contrast, manual scanning demonstrated lower reliability, with ICC values ranging from 0.40 to 0.70.

**Conclusion:** Robotic ultrasound scanning offers a more reliable method for scoliosis assessment than manual scanning. This enhanced reliability is attributed to the consistent probe placement facilitated by the robotic system. Consequently, robotic ultrasound may serve as a more dependable tool for monitoring scoliosis progression and for evaluating the efficacy of treatments such as bracing and physical therapy.

**Key Words:** Robotic ultrasound, scoliosis, reliability, vertebral body height ratio, vertebral body angle.

This study investigates the potential for extreme precipitation events in Earth's atmosphere during a hyper-thermal hothouse phase characterized by elevated CO2 levels and temperatures exceeding 30°C. Utilizing the Community Climate System Model version 1.4 (CCSM1.4), we conducted simulations with doubled CO2 concentrations and analyzed the resulting extremes in precipitation and sea level pressure. The hothouse atmosphere exhibited a significantly thicker structure, which amplified the hydrological cycle and led to a substantial increase in precipitation. While the spatial distribution of pressure systems remained largely consistent with current conditions, the pressure systems driving precipitation were more intense. Consequently, the frequency of extreme precipitation events increased markedly, with the most severe events occurring 10 to 100 times more often than in the present-day climate. These findings suggest that hothouse climates could be highly susceptible to episodic deluges. Furthermore, the ratio of extreme precipitation to the mean was found to be independent of the specific threshold used to define "extreme," a characteristic that aligns with the Pareto distribution. This indicates that the probability of extreme precipitation events in a hothouse climate follows a power law, a pattern also observed in modern extreme weather events. Ultimately, these results underscore the critical need to understand and mitigate the impacts of extreme weather events, particularly as the world progresses toward a hothouse state driven by anthropogenic climate change. The research also highlights the necessity of developing climate models capable of accurately simulating such extreme events. Finally, the study emphasizes the importance of analyzing extreme events across a spectrum of climate states, ranging from the current interglacial to future hothouse and icehouse conditions. This approach is essential for comprehending the full range of climate variability and for developing strategies to adapt to a changing climate. The paper concludes by outlining the implications of these findings for future research and policy-making. Additionally, the study addresses the limitations of the CCSM1.4 model in simulating extreme weather events and suggests potential avenues for improvement. The authors also discuss the ethical implications of extreme weather events and the role of climate change in exacerbating their frequency and intensity. The probability of transitioning from state $i$ to state $j$ in a single step is defined by the matrix $P_{ij}$. In a correlated random walk, the probability of moving from state $i$ to state $j$ after $n$ steps is represented by the matrix element $(P^n)_{ij}$. This study examines correlated random walks on a complete graph with $N$ nodes, where the transition probability matrix is given by $P_{ij} = p$ for $i \neq j$ and $P_{ii} = 1-p+Np$. We derive the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of this matrix, subsequently calculating $(P^n)_{ij}$ and demonstrating that the correlation in this model diminishes as $1/N$. Furthermore, we establish that the transition probability matrix for the corresponding strongly correlated random walk is singular. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we present a formula for the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix of a correlated random walk, which holds significance for analyzing the corresponding strongly correlated model. Finally, we outline a method for constructing the transition probability matrix of a correlated random walk given its correlation coefficient. This framework is applied to a two-state system, where we compute the correlation time and show that it scales as $1/(N-1)$. We also derive the probability of remaining in the same state after $n$ steps, illustrating that this model exhibits a crossover between the behaviors observed in the strongly correlated and weakly correlated random walk scenarios. The results are validated through numerical simulations. This work is part of a project aimed at developing a theoretical framework for the correlated random walk model to address the problem of anomalous diffusion. The paper concludes with an outline of the proposed framework. The HOL theorem prover has recently been updated to support a coinduction principle known as "by-clocked-coinduction," which offers a straightforward method for proving properties of potentially infinite data structures like streams. This paper explores various applications of this principle, including the verification of data structure and function definitions, the validation of refinement mappings, and the analysis of recursive functions. Additionally, we propose a novel application: the automated generation of corecursive functions based on clocked refinements. The implementation of this approach is demonstrated through several examples. The paper concludes by discussing the principle's limitations and outlining potential directions for future research. All examples provided in this work are available as HOL4 scripts.

This study introduces a data-driven approach to improve the prediction of instantaneous wall turbulence in incompressible flows using coherent structure-based models. The method addresses the inherent nonlinearity of the turbulent boundary layer by employing a recurrent neural network (RNN) to learn a nonlinear mapping from the instantaneous state of a low-order model to its future states. This enhanced RNN model is trained using data generated by a standard data-to-model framework. The results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly boosts the accuracy of instantaneous flow predictions, achieving a 20% improvement in the mean $C_p$ distribution compared to the conventional coherent structure-based modeling technique. Furthermore, the training process is computationally efficient, requiring only a few minutes on a single CPU core. These findings indicate that the approach holds substantial potential for enhancing the prediction of unsteady, complex flows. Additionally, the method is versatile and can be applied to various modeling strategies, including those utilizing proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) or dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) for flow modeling. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/Data-enhanced-structure-based-model.

Keywords: data-driven modeling, machine learning, wall turbulence, coherent structure-based modeling, recurrent neural network.

We investigate self-dual solitons within a deformed baby Skyrme model featuring Born-Infeld characteristics. Specifically, we examine both the D3 Born-Infeld model and the D5 baby Skyrme model, identifying self-dual configurations in each. We introduce a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna designed to generate a tailored electromagnetic environment that facilitates the creation of a new class of superior photon sources. This device is engineered to support a specific hybridized vibrational mode in silicon nanospheres, which couples with the localized surface plasmon mode of an attached gold nanoparticle. This interaction produces a unique subwavelength cavity mode that can be resonantly excited by an incoming laser. When a quantum emitter is placed within this cavity, it is driven into a new hybridized light-matter state. This state is characterized by a large Purcell factor, a high quality factor, and a strongly localized field, enabling the efficient and bright emission of single photons at a user-defined frequency. Furthermore, the inherent asymmetry of the nanoantenna allows for the unidirectional emission of these photons into free space. We demonstrate that this system can achieve a quality factor as high as 100, a Purcell factor exceeding 1000, and a radiation efficiency surpassing 90%. Additionally, we show that the unidirectional emission efficiency exceeds 90%, with the entire setup being fully tunable. These findings are supported by extensive theoretical and experimental data. Our proposed nanoantenna offers a promising platform for a wide array of applications, including quantum information processing, quantum communication, quantum sensing, and quantum-enhanced spectroscopy. The ability to precisely control the quantum emitter's interaction with the nanoantenna's electromagnetic field opens new avenues for advancing quantum technologies. Theoretical frameworks for granular matter have historically relied on the assumption that grain interactions are pairwise additive. However, recent experimental and numerical findings indicate that non-additive effects significantly influence the mechanical characteristics of granular assemblies. This study examines the anomalous screening effect, a phenomenon where an external force applied to a localized region of a rigid wall results in stress attenuation that decays more rapidly than predicted by standard theories. We validate the core tenets of the Anomalous Screening Theory, originally proposed by Oda and his colleagues, through both experimental and numerical investigations. Our results demonstrate that this effect is universal across all granular materials, though its magnitude varies depending on the specific material properties. Furthermore, we confirm the theory's validity by analyzing the influence of grain shape and size distribution on stress attenuation. Finally, we corroborate the Anomalous Screening Theory by examining the stress distribution within a force chain network. These findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the stress transmission mechanisms governing granular materials. Additionally, the proposed theory may prove valuable for developing new materials and technologies that leverage the unique properties of granular matter. This study investigates silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) using first-principles calculations. The system exhibits a stable, buckled honeycomb lattice structure. Doping with magnetic manganese (Mn) atoms induces a significant spin-orbit coupling effect within silicene, resulting in a magnetic exchange gap of 0.01 eV. Furthermore, Mn decoration breaks the system's inversion symmetry, generating a Rashba spin-orbit coupling term with a strength of 0.001 eV Å. These electronic characteristics are highly tunable through the application of external electric fields. Additionally, the analysis confirms that the interaction between Mn atoms and the substrate is weak, facilitating the formation of a van der Waals heterostructure. These findings suggest that Mn-decorated silicene on hBN is a promising candidate for spintronic applications. Finally, the study explores the potential for realizing a quantum Hall effect in this material under a perpendicular magnetic field. The proposed electronic properties of silicene on hBN offer a novel platform for investigating spin-orbit interactions and developing future spintronic devices. This study examines the connections between COVID-19 news coverage volume, case counts, fatalities, and audience size within U.S. local news outlets. Utilizing data from the COVID-19 News Coverage Database (covering 100 local outlets from January to May 2020) and the Local Television Audience Database (spanning 2019 to 2020), the research employs a two-stage econometric approach. The findings indicate that while the volume of news coverage does not influence the quantity of information received by audiences, both coverage volume and case numbers are positively correlated with audience size. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that higher coverage correlates with lower death rates, whereas the relationship between news coverage and case numbers remains ambiguous. These results suggest that local news coverage played a significant role in informing the public and mitigating the severity of the pandemic's impact. Additionally, the study demonstrates that local news audiences are not uniform; they vary based on the specific news outlet and the timing of the coverage. These insights offer valuable guidance for local news organizations on how to effectively balance resource allocation between news production and audience engagement. Finally, the paper discusses the potential implications of these results for future policy decisions.

**Keywords:** COVID-19; Local News; News Coverage; Audience Size; Audience Heterogeneity.

This study examines the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) for calculating forces within particle systems, specifically addressing its accuracy in preserving angular momentum. While FMM offers a significant speed advantage over direct methods by reducing computational cost from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$, it traditionally incurs truncation errors due to approximating multipole expansions with finite terms. We demonstrate that these errors are not merely artifacts of the expansion but stem from the selection of source points at the centers of spatial cells. By shifting these source points away from the cell centers, we show that the algorithm can achieve exact conservation of angular momentum. Furthermore, we establish that this modification introduces only a negligible increase in computational expense. Our approach is applicable to the standard FMM algorithm and can be extended to various acceleration techniques. We validate these findings using a simple yet representative model of gravitational interactions. Finally, we explore the implications of this result for acceleration methods that maintain consistency with angular momentum conservation. Our findings indicate that the proposed adjustment to FMM is compatible with several such methods, including the Shifted Inverse Distance algorithm and the Recursive Image algorithm. Additionally, we present a straightforward technique to correct angular momentum in FMM-based methods that do natively conserve it, such as Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics. This correction involves solving a single linear equation, resulting in minimal computational overhead. We conclude that the proposed modifications to FMM are both straightforward and highly effective. We anticipate that these enhancements will facilitate the development of more efficient and accurate acceleration methods in the future. This study presents a search for Higgs boson pair production in association with a vector boson ( VH) utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis examines data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, collected with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$ during 2015 and 2016. The investigation targets the decay channels where one Higgs boson decays into a $b$-quark pair and the other into a $W$ or $Z$ boson, which subsequently decays leptonically. The analysis covers the $VV$ final states, where V represents a $W$ or $Z$ boson, and examines scenarios where the bosons decay into leptonic or hadronic final states. The results are interpreted within the framework of the Standard Model and the simplified $tt^*$ model. No significant excess over the expected background is observed. The 95% confidence level upper limit on the Higgs boson pair production cross section is determined to be 1.1 times the Standard Model prediction. Additionally, the simplified $tt^*$ model coupling parameter is constrained to a range of $0.15 \leq f_{tt^*} \leq 1.5$ at a 95% confidence level. This represents the most stringent constraint to date for the $tt^*$ model. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that incorporating a kinematic discriminant based on the Higgs boson candidate mass distribution enhances the sensitivity of the search. The resulting mass distribution for the $VV$ channel shows a significance of 1.1 standard deviations, corresponding to an expected significance of 1.0 standard deviations under background-only and signal-plus-background hypotheses. This study examines the detection of hate speech in Hindi and Bengali, two major Indo-European languages. We present the inaugural large-scale dataset for this purpose, comprising 1,000 user comments each from social media platforms, annotated by human judges. Our analysis reveals that while the distribution of positive and negative labels is balanced in Hindi, Bengali exhibits a significant imbalance. We evaluate several neural network architectures, demonstrating that a bidirectional LSTM outperforms both bidirectional GRU and unidirectional LSTM variants. Furthermore, we investigate the application of transfer learning to address the label imbalance issue in Bengali. The dataset and experimental findings will be made available to the research community. Finally, we discuss the ethical challenges inherent in hate speech detection, particularly the risk of inadvertently amplifying harmful stereotypes. This work was conducted as part of the inaugural Data Science for Social Good Hackathon. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishgupta1997/Indo-European-Hate-Speech. Time projection chambers (TPCs) utilizing ionization in gas detectors offer a robust method for particle identification by measuring the time and position of ionization events. This study introduces observables designed to identify the recoil nucleus resulting from a detected particle. We demonstrate that these observables can distinguish nuclear recoils from electron recoils with high precision, even when using low-quality data. Furthermore, we show that a simple likelihood ratio constructed from these observables surpasses the performance of existing observables in the literature. This approach is applicable to TPCs employing gas detectors with three-dimensional spatial resolution, such as the high-definition TPCs currently under development for dark matter research. Our findings indicate that a detector with a 1 cm active volume could achieve a nuclear recoil detection sensitivity comparable to that of the LUX experiment. Additionally, we demonstrate that these observables can be extended to include information regarding the total number of ionization electrons. This enhancement allows for the rejection of nuclear recoils generated by low-energy particles, a capability that could significantly improve the sensitivity of dark matter experiments. Finally, we illustrate that these observables can be utilized to determine the nuclear recoil energy spectrum for dark matter candidates with masses ranging from 1 GeV to 100 TeV. This analysis reveals that a detector with a 10 cm active volume could achieve a sensitivity similar to that of the XENON1T experiment. These results suggest that the high-definition TPC concept is viable for dark matter searches targeting sub-GeV WIMP candidates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the technique can be adapted to extract the nuclear recoil spectrum from data collected by the XENON1T experiment. Our analysis indicates that XENON1T could achieve a sensitivity of approximately $10^{-10}$ per nucleon for a dark matter cross section of $10^{-40}$ cm$^2$. This sensitivity is comparable to the best current limits for sub-GeV dark matter candidates. Finally, we show that the high-definition TPC concept could achieve a sensitivity of $10^{-11}$ per nucleon, representing a tenfold improvement over the XENON1T capabilities. These findings underscore the potential of high-definition TPCs to advance the search for sub-GeV dark matter. Manifolds characterized by negative sectional curvature are prevalent across mathematics and physics, with the hyperbolic space serving as the primary example. These structures possess distinctive properties, including an abundance of geodesic curves and a lack of conjugate points. This paper investigates the statistical characteristics of geodesics within negatively curved manifolds, specifically focusing on their distributional features and the temporal evolution of their geometric invariants. We demonstrate that as the curvature approaches zero, the distribution of geodesic angles converges to a Gaussian distribution. Furthermore, we establish that the temporal evolution of their geometric invariants follows a power law, a finding that holds significant implications for the study of random field manifolds. By applying these results to the analysis of random field manifolds, we reveal that their geodesic distributions exhibit heavy tails, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the presence of cusps. Additionally, we examine the impact of cusp removal on the temporal evolution of geometric invariants, demonstrating that this process can accelerate the evolution by several orders of magnitude. These findings are particularly relevant for understanding the dynamics of random field manifolds in the context of cosmology and general relativity. Finally, we provide a comprehensive numerical analysis of geodesics on the Poincaré ball, Poincaré upper half-plane, and the Poincaré cube, utilizing the geodesic equations derived in this work. Our numerical results align closely with the theoretical predictions, thereby validating the accuracy of our approach. The code utilized in this study is publicly accessible on GitHub. Specifically, we establish that within the periodic context, LIFO achieves optimal $O(\log n)$ performance, yet it fails to be robust, as evidenced by the existence of a specific family of inputs that degrade its behavior. This study investigates spin-dependent transport within armchair graphene nanoribbons (AGNRs) by integrating a Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC) term with an external electric field. Utilizing the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism, we analyze how various parameters influence the system's transmission and spin polarization. Our findings indicate that the Rashba SOC parameter ($\lambda$) can be tuned to achieve both spin-filtering and spin-switching behaviors. Furthermore, we observe that the transmission characteristics of AGNRs exhibit strong sensitivity to $\lambda$, a phenomenon attributed to the interaction between the Rashba SOC and the transverse confinement potential. Additionally, we demonstrate that the spin polarization of AGNRs can be significantly enhanced by adjusting the width of the nanoribbons. Finally, we propose a specific AGNR configuration capable of producing a nearly 100% spin-polarized current. These conclusions hold significant promise for advancing the development of spintronic devices based on AGNRs. Finally, we outline the potential applications of these findings in the context of spintronics. Furthermore, the $v_1$ of $\pi^-$ was found to be approximately 10% larger than that of $\pi^+$, a result consistent with the quark charge sequence. These findings indicate that the initial spatial anisotropy dominates the generation of directed flow in heavy ion collisions. Additionally, the systematic uncertainties associated with the initial conditions and the viscous hydrodynamic model were quantified. Finally, the results suggest that the initial pressure gradient is the main factor responsible for the directed flow of light hadrons. These conclusions are expected to guide future research into the initial conditions of heavy ion collisions. The analysis code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/STAR-BayesianAnalysis. This study introduces a sparse-grid adaptive spectral method designed to solve the linear Koopman operator equation for estimating the state of nonlinear dynamical systems. By employing sparse-grid collocation, the approach mitigates the curse of dimensionality inherent in traditional spectral techniques. Furthermore, the framework utilizes the e-SVD algorithm to adaptively refine the basis function set, thereby enhancing both computational efficiency and estimation accuracy. The method's efficacy is validated through two numerical case studies: a linear system with process and measurement noise, and a nonlinear pendulum system under noisy conditions. Results demonstrate that the proposed sparse-grid adaptive spectral method surpasses the finite-horizon spectral method in both accuracy and computational speed. Additionally, it outperforms the e-SVD algorithm, achieving superior accuracy while significantly reducing the number of basis functions required. Finally, the method successfully estimates the state of a nonlinear system, confirming its broad applicability. These findings indicate that the sparse-grid adaptive spectral method is highly effective for estimating nonlinear systems. [Abstract] This paper proposes a sparse-grid adaptive spectral method to address the challenge of estimating states in nonlinear dynamical systems. The core of this approach is a sparse-grid collocation technique that circumvents the curse of dimensionality typically associated with conventional spectral methods. To further improve accuracy and computational efficiency, the method incorporates adaptive spectral techniques. The adaptive scheme dynamically adjusts the size of the basis function set, ensuring that the resulting model remains both accurate and efficient. To validate the method's effectiveness, two numerical examples are provided: a linear system with additive process and measurement noise, and a nonlinear pendulum system with multiplicative noise. The results demonstrate that the proposed sparse-grid adaptive spectral method outperforms the finite-horizon spectral method in both accuracy and computational speed. Moreover, compared to the e-SVD algorithm, the proposed method requires fewer basis functions to achieve higher accuracy. Finally, the method successfully estimates the state of a nonlinear system, confirming its broad applicability. These findings suggest that the sparse-grid adaptive spectral method is highly effective for estimating nonlinear systems. This paper introduces a novel method utilizing exterior complex scaling (ECS) to investigate atomic and molecular systems subjected to strong direct current (DC) fields. We demonstrate that the molecular polarization curve for H$_2^+$ exhibits a linear relationship with respect to the field strength within weak DC regimes, a finding that aligns with the classical electric field applied to a dipole oscillator. Furthermore, our results indicate that the DC field induces a shift in the effective nuclear charge of the 1s orbital, a phenomenon that can be interpreted as a modification of the atomic potential experienced by electrons. This orbital adjustment is anticipated to play a crucial role in determining the ionization dynamics of atoms and molecules under strong DC fields. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the electron density distribution for the H atom across various field strengths, revealing that the electron density shifts in the direction of the applied field. Finally, we show that the DC field induces a non-zero permanent electric dipole moment in the ground state of the H atom, a property that remains absent in the absence of the field. These findings are expected to be applicable to other atomic and molecular systems. Our study demonstrates that the ECS approach offers a robust framework for analyzing atomic and molecular systems in strong DC fields, with potential applications extending to alternating current (AC) fields. The computational code implementing this method is publicly accessible. Our results provide a foundation for future research into the ionization dynamics of atoms and molecules exposed to strong DC fields. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential applications of these findings in fields such as laser physics, plasma physics, and astrophysics. We also outline several avenues for future research, including the application of the ECS method to more complex atomic and molecular systems, as well as the study of electron correlation effects and relativistic effects under strong DC fields. Additionally, we propose exploring the ECS method's applicability to systems involving multiple electrons and multiple nuclei. Finally, we suggest that these findings could have significant implications for various scientific disciplines, including laser physics, plasma physics, and astrophysics. The ECS approach is expected to be a valuable tool for analyzing atomic and molecular systems in strong DC fields, with potential applications in laser physics, plasma physics, and astrophysics. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, including the application of the ECS method to more complex atomic and molecular systems, as well as the study of electron correlation effects and relativistic effects under strong DC fields. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a well-established iterative method for resolving the Schr\"odinger problem, which involves finding a solution proportional to the product of two given vectors. While its convergence is guaranteed when a solution exists, the algorithm's behavior in cases where no solution is possible has not been rigorously analyzed. This paper demonstrates that, despite the absence of a solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm converges to a specific limit that is uniquely determined by the problem's data. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithm exhibits linear convergence in this scenario. These findings are derived through the application of recent results concerning the Moreau envelope and proximal point methods. Additionally, we explore a connection between the Sinkhorn problem and the classical problem of finding the best low-rank approximation of a matrix. Finally, we validate our theoretical contributions with numerical experiments. The code utilized in this study is accessible at \url{https://github.com/jeanfrancoisbonnet1980/Sinkhorn_no_solution}. We investigate the dynamics of a central localized state within a ring of $N$ coupled, nonidentical, and dissipative units, demonstrating that the system's behavior is governed by the distribution of eigenvalues of the coupling matrix. Specifically, we show that the rate at which the localized state decays to the steady-state solution is determined by the real part of the eigenvalue with the smallest magnitude. Furthermore, the dynamics transition from periodic to chaotic as this dominant eigenvalue crosses the imaginary axis. Finally, we establish that the primary characteristics of the system's dynamics can be accurately captured by reducing it to a two-dimensional model. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of both continuous and discrete systems. The methodology is broadly applicable to various contexts, including arrays of Josephson junctions, optical waveguides, and networks of excitable cells. Additionally, the results offer valuable insights for the design of novel devices and systems. For instance, the periodic dynamics observed in our study can be harnessed to generate a train of pulses with a specific, tunable period. This is achieved by selecting an appropriate central unit and adjusting the coupling strength to ensure the eigenvalue with the minimal real part lies close to the imaginary axis. Consequently, the pulse train exhibits a long period that can be finely tuned by adjusting the coupling strength. This capability is particularly advantageous for applications requiring pulse trains with extended periods. Moreover, the periodic dynamics can be converted into chaotic dynamics by introducing a small perturbation to the central unit, thereby enabling the generation of a chaotic train of pulses. This chaotic train possesses a broad spectrum of periods, offering a mechanism for producing pulses with very short intervals. These results are also applicable to the design of chaotic neural networks, where the central cell functions as a neuron capable of firing pulses with a wide range of periods. The proposed approach is demonstrated using a central FitzHugh-Nagumo neuron embedded in a ring of identical neurons. Finally, we highlight that the chaotic dynamics of the central unit can be utilized to synchronize the dynamics of the entire system. This is accomplished by introducing a small perturbation to the central unit and adjusting the coupling strength so that the eigenvalue with the smallest real part is near the imaginary axis. Under these conditions, the central unit's dynamics synchronize with the rest of the system, allowing the central neuron to act as a chaotic driving force for the network. This paper identifies conditions on the parameters within the coefficients of Bessel functions to ensure that the resulting functions belong to the class $P[\alpha,\beta]$. Additionally, the study derives inequalities for Bessel function coefficients and determines the radius of convexity. Finally, it establishes the radius of the Janowski class and the radius of convexity for Bessel functions under the condition $\left| \frac{z f^{\prime \prime}(z)}{f(z)-\beta} \right| < k < 1$. These findings are illustrated through specific instances of Bessel functions. Furthermore, the study examines the inclusion of generalized Bessel functions within the class $P[\alpha,\beta]$ and investigates the inclusion relations between two generalized Bessel functions. Finally, the radius of convexity for these generalized forms is determined. The results presented here extend and improve upon existing literature. Additionally, the inclusion relations between the generalized Bessel functions and the class $P[\alpha,\beta]$ are illustrated through numerical examples. Urban environments are renowned for their social interactions and the exchange of diverse ideas, which are thought to drive innovation and creativity. However, the COVID-19 pandemic and its associated restrictions, including stay-at-home orders and social distancing, significantly curtailed these interactions. This study examines how the pandemic altered the frequency and diversity of encounters within cities. Utilizing anonymized mobile phone data from 100 cities across 14 nations, we observed that the diversity of income-related interactions declined in 60% of these cities. This reduction was primarily driven by a drop in the number of interactions with individuals from different income brackets. These findings remained consistent even after accounting for lockdown policies and pre-pandemic economic conditions. Furthermore, the decline in income diversity was more pronounced in cities with higher pre-pandemic economic inequality. These results underscore the pivotal role of urban interactions in the functioning of cities and suggest that safeguarding these connections is essential for mitigating the pandemic's adverse effects. Additionally, the research offers a novel method for analyzing urban encounters that can be applied to investigate other phenomena. Finally, our findings highlight the potential of mobile data to deepen our understanding of urban dynamics. (Note: This research was conducted prior to the full implementation of lockdowns.) This study evaluates various nonlinear field-split preconditioners designed for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media, utilizing the open-source software MOOSE. The investigated methods include a standard field-split preconditioner enhanced with a nonlinear fixed-point smoother, a nonlinear Schur complement preconditioner, a nonlinear additive Schwarz preconditioner, and a nonlinear multigrid preconditioner. All these techniques employ a nonlinear field-splitting approach to handle the two-phase capillary pressure term within the heterogeneous permeability field. Additionally, a nonlinear multigrid preconditioner that neglects capillary pressure is examined for comparison. The research focuses on a widely used model for heterogeneous porous media, where permeability varies according to a lognormal distribution. We assess these preconditioners across a range of scenarios, including varying levels of heterogeneity, saturation-dependent relative permeability, and different grid resolutions. Our findings indicate that the nonlinear field-split preconditioner is highly effective for this model, demonstrating robustness across different grid sizes and strong scalability on high-performance computing systems. However, its performance degrades significantly when capillary pressure is neglected. In contrast, the nonlinear multigrid preconditioner that ignores capillary pressure exhibits superior performance in that specific scenario. Finally, we explore the potential of integrating the field-split approach with a multigrid method that accounts for capillary pressure. This combined nonlinear field-split multigrid preconditioner shows promising results, though further investigation is required to fully understand its behavior. The source code for all tested preconditioners is publicly accessible via the MOOSE framework. Furthermore, we provide a detailed guide on selecting an appropriate preconditioner for a given problem. We introduce a new class of optical cavities characterized by chiral properties arising from the geometry of their reflecting walls. By employing single-handedness (SH) and multi-handedness (MH) curves, we demonstrate that these cavities can sustain robust, backscattering-free unidirectional propagation. Specifically, we show that the single-mode region of an SH curve is broader than that of a traditional circular cavity, while the MH case offers an additional degree of freedom for mode engineering. Furthermore, we identify that specific configurations of SH and MH curves can eliminate degeneracy, resulting in non-constant Gaussian curvature within the single-mode region. Finally, we propose that these cavities are well-suited for applications such as single-phased optical oscillators and sensors. To validate these findings, we provide a practical example of an SH curve cavity utilizing a reflective metamaterial wall. This example confirms that the single-mode region is substantial and that the proposed design achieves a record-breaking quality factor of $10^{10}$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the cavity exhibits a record level of chiral transmission, with a figure of chirality reaching $0.9999999999$. We anticipate that this work will inspire the development of novel cavity designs with distinctive geometrical and optical characteristics. We demonstrate that the $c<1$ $c_1=a$ singlet CFT, which arises from the limit $Q\to0$ of the Liouville CFT with $c_1=a$ background, is dual to the same $c<1$ JT gravity in AdS$_2$ with a negative cosmological constant $\Lambda=-\mu$. This duality holds in the presence of a $c_1=a$ background charge, corresponding to a $\mu$-dependent boundary action in the dual JT gravity. Furthermore, we show that the Liouville CFT with $c_1=a$ background charge can be formulated as a two-dimensional reduction of a specific supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. Consequently, the $c<1$ $c_1=a$ singlet CFT is equivalent to the two-dimensional reduction of a specific supermatrix model. Finally, we establish that this supermatrix model is dual to the supergravity limit of the $c<1$ $c_1=a$ JT gravity. This latter theory describes a two-dimensional reduction of $c_1=a$ $c=1$ string theory in the presence of a background charge, where the cosmological constant $\Lambda=-\mu$ is determined by the background charge. In this framework, the $c<1$ $c_1=a$ JT gravity corresponds to a $c=1$ string theory with a negative cosmological constant $\Lambda=-\mu$. We also examine the relationship between the supermatrix model and the $c=1$ string theory with $\Lambda=-\mu$. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ correspondence. This work is a joint effort with J. Teschner. Additionally, we thank A. Maloney, A. Sen, and S. The Alcubierre solution represents a spacetime geometry enabling superluminal travel via localized faster-than-light warp drives. While originally a vacuum solution, we demonstrate that incorporating a perfect fluid with an equation of state $p=\rho/2$ alongside a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ allows for a broader class of solutions. This class is defined by two arbitrary functions of time, $\alpha(t)$ and $\beta(t)$, which govern the bubble's velocity and the rate of change of the bubble's proper volume. We further prove that this class constitutes the most general possible solution when a cosmological constant is present. Finally, we examine the energy requirements for operating such a warp drive within this class of solutions. These findings suggest that perfect fluid warp drive solutions are more feasible than previously thought, as they require less energy than both the original Alcubierre solution and more recent vacuum generalizations. Additionally, we show that these solutions can be derived using the inverse method. Finally, we explore the physical implications of these results. This work is part of a series investigating warp drive solutions within the framework of general relativity. For context, see our companion paper [arXiv:2009.00001]. We introduce a two-stage spin-dependent detection method that leverages the high sensitivity of spin dephasing to local electric field fluctuations. This approach enables the measurement of motional state distributions and heating rates for individual ions within a 2D Coulomb crystal. By applying this technique to a single $^{171}$Yb$^+$ ion, we demonstrate its efficacy in distinguishing between thermal and non-thermal state distributions. Furthermore, we establish that spin dephasing serves as a robust probe for heating rates, with observed rates aligning closely with those predicted by a simple three-body model. These findings underscore the method's utility for characterizing the non-thermal dynamics of ions in quantum simulation experiments. Our results indicate that spin dephasing can detect heating rates as low as $10^{-3}$ quanta per millisecond, surpassing the sensitivity of direct ion imaging. Additionally, we show that this technique is readily adaptable to other atomic and hybrid quantum systems. Finally, we outline potential applications, including the investigation of thermalization in quantum simulators and the development of quantum sensors. This work was published in *Phys. Rev. Terahertz sum frequency generation (THz-SFG) spectroscopy has been utilized to investigate the vibrational modes of a single silver nanoparticle. To model these findings, we employ a fully quantum mechanical approach that incorporates both chemical and electromagnetic effects. Our results indicate that the observed vibrational modes are primarily determined by the specific crystallographic facets of the nanoparticle. Furthermore, the symmetry of these modes is dictated by the orientation of the nanoparticle relative to the THz radiation polarization. Additionally, we demonstrate that the nanoparticle's position within the tip-sample gap is a critical factor influencing the experimental outcomes. These insights provide a robust framework for interpreting and designing future experiments involving THz-SFG on single nanoparticles. This methodology is also applicable to other techniques, such as tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS), which share similar physical principles. Specifically, for TERS, we show that the excitation of surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) on the nanoparticle surface is contingent upon the polarization of the laser light. Finally, we examine the impact of the nanoparticle's crystallographic orientation on the resulting TERS spectra. These conclusions are derived from simulations utilizing a realistic nanoparticle model. The methodology presented here is broadly applicable to nanoparticles of varying shapes and sizes. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for elucidating the complex interplay between chemical and electromagnetic effects in TERS. This is particularly significant for advancing the field toward achieving single-molecule sensitivity. To achieve this, it is essential to understand the specific facets of the nanoparticle that are primarily enhanced by the tip. Our simulations reveal that the local electromagnetic field is amplified at certain facets more than others, a phenomenon that can be predicted by analyzing the TERS spectra. These findings are corroborated by experimental data. Consequently, this approach offers a pathway to achieve single-molecule sensitivity in TERS. This is accomplished by employing a tip with an atomic-scale apex and a nanoparticle with a well-defined crystallographic orientation. Such a configuration ensures that the local electromagnetic field is concentrated on a specific facet, thereby enhancing the vibrational modes of a single molecule. This strategy is expected to be applicable to a wide range of molecules. The methodology is implemented using the Quantum ESPRESSO software package. Ammonium sulfate ((NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$) exhibits a large entropy-driven electric-caloric effect, yet the origin of this entropy change remains unclear. This study investigates the source of this entropy variation by analyzing the entropy of configurational disorder within the (NH$_4$)$_2$ groupings. By combining experimental data with first-principles molecular dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that the entropy change stems from the ordering of (NH$_4$) dipoles. Furthermore, we show that this dipole ordering is facilitated by the ferroelectric phase transition occurring in (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$. These findings offer a fundamental understanding of entropy-driven molecular caloric materials. Additionally, our results indicate that (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$ could be utilized as a high-temperature solid-state entropy storage medium. Finally, we propose that other materials with similar crystal structures and ferroelectric phase transitions could also display entropy-driven caloric effects. This research expands the scope of entropy-driven caloric materials and provides a foundation for the design of new molecular caloric compounds.
